title: Negotiating with the Angolan Coast: Recreational Fishing in Colonial Luanda (1945–1975)
abstract: This article contributes to and expands the environmental history of recreational fishing through examining the development of recreational fishing in late colonial Luanda, Angola, 1945–1975. It draws on colonial archives, newspapers, tourism magazines, specialised fishing periodicals and oral testimonies to argue that recreational fishing developed through processes of dwelling in different coastal environments as practitioners and practices took shape in relation to their ecological conditions and possibilities. On the more accessible northern coast of Luanda, fishing was closely intertwined with everyday leisure, sociability and food provisioning, while the more environmentally heterogeneous southern coast demanded greater mobility and more specialised forms of angling. In the absence of systematic scientific research on marine ecosystems, recreational fishing relied on understandings of coastal dynamics and drew upon multiple layers of local knowledge. By foregrounding the changing relationships between recreational fishing, coastal environments and ecological processes, the article also contributes to broader discussions of human–environment interactions, tourism and coastal leisure.

title: Imagining Japanese Technofutures – The Role of Futurology and Science Fiction in Shaping the Information Society
abstract: The original roots of the information society (jōhō shakai) are clearly Japanese and date back to the year 1963. The concept was developed in the context of a private study group circle spearheaded by the anthropologist Umesao Tadao, including members like the science fiction writer Komatsu Sakyō and the futurologist Hayashi Yūjirō. Drawing on the methodology of science and technology studies (STS), I will show how the ideological narrative underlying Umesao’s original theory on the information industries was condensed into a sociotechnical imaginary (STI) in the years from 1963 to the end of the 1970s. This article explains why the narrative was so successful and how the Expo 1970 in Osaka served as a showcase for the public performance and stabilization of the STI. The article argues that this contributed to its lasting impact on the way in which Japanese technofutures were imagined, based on the premise of a techno-centered society.

title: Transimperial Manhood: Theodore Roosevelt and Gendered Politics in US-Japanese Relations
abstract: The gender ideology of no other US president has elicited as much scholarly fascination as that of Theodore Roosevelt. Historians have closely analyzed his transformation from sickly child to big stick-wielding outdoorsman, highlighting how his overbearing father, frontier experience, and the societal transformations of the Gilded Age shaped an idiosyncratic gendered worldview that guided his political decisions.1 Neil Cogan even argues that manhood was Roosevelt’s central political organizing principle, linking progressivism and global power concerns over civilizational struggle within a common gendered vision.2 So far, this literature has treated this vision as a domestic construct rooted in US socialization and projected outward through political actions. Such a reading overlooks the realities of the United States in which Roosevelt came into political maturity: an ascending empire embedded in global networks of shared imperial knowledge, culture, and practice. An avid reader and passionate traveler, Roosevelt actively and enthusiastically participated in this global system. How did it impact his gendered formation? What does this tell us about the role of gendered knowledge circulation in shaping imperial diplomatic culture?

title: Financing Water Services through Ottoman Cash Waqfs in Rumelia
abstract: This article examines how cash waqfs financed water services in Ottoman Rumelia (the empire’s Balkan provinces) from the sixteenth to the early twentieth century, as a contribution to both waqf studies and environmental history. It draws on a primary-source database of 953 Rumelian endowment records, from which 165 cash waqfs linked to water provision were identified and analysed. It makes three arguments. First, these foundations formed a significant, regionally differentiated mechanism of public provision: they supported fountains and waterways above all, but also bridges, sebils and mixed service clusters. Second, their importance lay less in establishing water services than in sustaining them: by converting preserved capital into recurring income for maintenance, wages and repair, cash waqfs operated as an institutionalised mechanism of sustainability. Third, the geography of this provision followed the environmental and urban structure of the Balkans, so that mountain, riverine and port settings produced distinct service profiles.

title: From Eradication to Adaptation: The Colorado Potato Beetle in Cold War Czechoslovakia
abstract: This article examines the Colorado potato beetle in postwar Czechoslovakia as a case through which to explore the relationship between environmental processes and socialist environmental governance. While the beetle was widely framed in Cold War propaganda as an ‘American’ agent of sabotage, the paper argues that its political significance cannot be reduced to ideological projection. Rather, it emerged from the interaction between the insect’s biological characteristics and the state’s efforts to monitor, control, and eradicate it. Drawing on archival sources from agricultural and party institutions, the analysis traces how the spread of the beetle in the early 1950s was transformed from an agronomic problem into an issue of political urgency and security. It shows how systems of monitoring and mapping, mass mobilisation campaigns, and large-scale chemical interventions were deployed in response, while the beetle’s capacity for rapid reproduction and repeated re-infestation continually exposed the limits of these strategies. Conceptually, the article engages with recent work in environmental history and more-than-human approaches to examine how nonhuman life can shape perception, political interpretation, and practices of governance. From this perspective, the Colorado potato beetle can be understood not only as an object of discourse but as a persistent ecological presence that influenced both the practices and expectations of state intervention. title: The First World War and Japan’s cabinet system: how the conflict changed the perception and reception of foreign constitutional models by Japanese elites (1912–1920)
abstract: The modern Japanese state, built on the Meiji Constitution (1889–1947), has long been understood as inspired by a Prussian model. Recent historiography, however, emphasises a paradigm shift in Japanese national identity after the First World War and the development of party politics in the 1920s. How did the experience of this conflict alter the vision of European constitutional frameworks and the choice of foreign models for interpreting Japan’s own political institutions? This article, while focusing on the cabinet system, addresses this question by analysing constitutional commentaries and reform projects by scholars, statesmen, and journalists across three chronological stages. First, it shows that doctrinal debates from 1912 to 1914 were polarised by ideologies favouring the German or British models. Second, it observes essential changes in information pipelines during the war, a detachment from Germany, and increasing praise for Britain’s resilience. Third, it argues that reform projects by influential actors in the war’s immediate aftermath were designed after the United Kingdom’s recent institutional evolutions. These considerations shed light on an early stage of the global dissemination of the Westminster model and suggest its influence went beyond the Dominions and the post-Second World War Commonwealth.

title: Torii Ryūzō’s anthropometric measurements and photography in colonial Korea
abstract: Several historians have analyzed anthropologist Torii Ryuzō's ethnographic research across East Asia and the Pacific, including his use of photography in conducting fieldwork. However, scholars have largely overlooked his interest in physical anthropology in the early part of his career. This article investigates Torii's anthropometric research in Korea during the 1910s to show that, despite a large amount of data collected through years of fieldwork, institutional and technical reasons prevented his research from being part of the scholarly dialogue in the following years. Torii was seeking to combine anthropometric measurements with photography to innovate a research method that would critically engage contemporary European anthropological scholarship, through the combination of qualitative and quantitative approaches. However, from the 1920s, physical anthropology in Japan underwent a major shift with the widespread adoption of Rudolf Martin's anthropometric methods. With Keijō Imperial University in colonial Korea serving as one of the important research hubs, anatomists emphasizing precise measurements and statistical analysis dominated Japanese physical anthropology. Consequently, despite its scale and the attempt to arrive at an innovative methodology, Torii never managed to publish his anthropometry data or anthropometric photographs from Korea. This article thus shows, through tracing the disappearance of Torii's physical anthropology from academic discourse, …

title: Following East African cowries: Currency supply, transoceanic exchange, and monetary transformation in the nineteenth century
abstract: Abstract This article recentres East Africa in the global history of cowrie shells by tracing the trajectories of Monetaria annulus —the East African cowrie species—across interconnected monetary arenas in the nineteenth century. Situating African monetary history within transoceanic processes, it argues that the ‘great cowrie inflation’ in West Africa was closely tied to the reorganization of procurement networks, labour regimes, and commercial infrastructures in the Western Indian Ocean. Viewed from Zanzibar, the massive export of East African cowries emerges as the outcome of intersecting processes: price fluctuations in Maldivian shells, the expansion of the palm oil trade, extractive labour networks, and imperial interests. The article further shows that the same infrastructures were later reoriented toward the Great Lakes region, tracing how a single commodity connected East and West Africa, the Indian Ocean, and the Atlantic world. Following cowries across these overlapping spaces demonstrates that monetary history—wherever it is written—cannot be fully understood without attending to the supply-side infrastructures that made money available.

title: Regionalising development: UN expertise and the making of a pan-Arab welfare field, 1949–59
abstract: Abstract In August 1949, the first Social Research Seminar for the Arab States convened in Beirut; five further seminars followed over the next decade. Drawing on Arabic-language seminar proceedings and UN archival records, this article recovers these largely overlooked gatherings to analyse how a distinct regional developmental field took shape in the post-war Arab East. UN institutional uncertainty in the late 1940s allowed the Arab League to capture this format, to authenticate global development through civilisational framing—most visibly in a lexical shift from emancipatory inʿāsh (reinvigoration) to custodial riʿāya (guardianship)—and to consolidate a self-sustaining professional field. The resulting regional arena mediated between global circulation and national implementation while proving durably compatible with the authoritarian welfare regimes emerging across the region.

title: Dystopia as Forecast: How the Japanese Privacy Movement Contested an Imagined Data State, 1970s–1990s
abstract: During the 1970s, as computerization became central to Japan’s public administration, the state advanced a sociotechnical imaginary of an efficient, digitally unified information society, built on integrating personal data and culminating in a proposed national identification number. In response, a social movement emerged to contest the concentration of informational power in state and corporate systems. This article argues that the movement is best understood as a politics of anticipation. It mobilized against a data state that did not yet exist, contesting the imaginary as a claim about the future, not present harms. Drawing on imported and projected examples, activists fought on two fronts, protection of personal data and access to government information, in an anticipatory contest that co-produced Japan’s data-governance regime. Tracing the movement from the 1972 founding of the Central Council for Opposing the National ID System and Protecting Privacy through census resistance and activists’ entry into local government, the article shows that the feared data state arrived only in constrained form, hedged by the oversight the movement had demanded. Neither the imaginary’s triumph nor the movement’s victory, the resulting settlement turns on the question it first raised: who should control the collection, circulation, and use of personal information?

title: Imagining a Cashless Future for Japan: Sociotechnical Imaginaries in a Consensus-Driven Society
abstract: This article examines Japan’s transition toward a cashless society through the lens of sociotechnical imaginaries, highlighting how technological and social factors interact in a consensus-driven context. The analysis focuses on six editions of the Cashless Roadmap (2019–2024) published by the semi-governmental Payments Japan Association (PJA), which brings together state, industry, and consumer perspectives. Employing content analysis, the article identifies four dominant imaginaries shaping Japan’s cashless future: seamless and invisible payments; digital infrastructure as a driver of social transformation; cashless as a new lifestyle; and inclusive, equitable digital participation for all. These imaginaries overlap and evolve in response to events such as the COVID-19 pandemic, government incentive programs, and international benchmarks, particularly China’s model of QR-based payments. Findings show that while globally circulating visions of data monetization, payment growth, and user experience resonate in Japan, they are reframed to emphasize trust, transparency, and social cohesion. The discussion highlights both synergies and tensions among the four imaginaries. Their complementarities reinforce a multi-dimensional strategy for efficiency, lifestyle transformation, and inclusion, aligned to support national renewal. Ultimately, the Cashless Roadmaps fulfill a performative role, mobilizing diverse stakeholders and embedding cashless payment within Japan’s broader …

title: Come a long way: The global historian’s craft, twenty years on
abstract: Abstract Twenty years after the founding of the Journal of Global History , this anniversary article takes stock of global history: its trajectory, its markers of disciplinary maturity, its political sense of purpose, and the difficulties and limits of the enterprise. Concerns after 2016 that global history might lose its relevance in a changing political climate have, thus far, not been borne out. By many measures, global history is both a flourishing field and an influential sensibility. Its enduring contribution, this article argues, lies in how it has helped, and continues to help, bring about a fuller, more accurate, and more complete understanding of the ever-incomplete ‘selection of facts’ that constitutes history, our humble truth. Twenty years on, global historians know their field’s limitations but also its value. They know that they have brought the world into history—and that this is no small thing.

title: Toppling coloniality: interventions on tainted monuments toward an open future
abstract: The article examines how monuments tied to colonial histories can operate as instruments of the ‘colonization of the mind’, and how interventions on them can become anti-colonial practices. Drawing on decolonial theory and recent scholarship on tainted monuments, it argues that commemorations do not merely depict the past; as objects that dwell in the temporality of coloniality, they authorize present hierarchies and future-oriented commitments, often through seemingly neutral artistic forms. The paper maps distinct intervention repertoires based on Latin American cases mainly from 2020–2023, and identifies differences in approaches related to agency, temporality, and visibility. It proposes six criteria for interventions with anti-colonial force: broad participation, institutional avowal, bottom-up deliberation, multi-dimensional attention to affect and intimate attachments, enduring and dynamic visibility, and explicit display of temporal continuities between colonial violence and contemporary oppressive structures. The paper concludes that keeping intervened monuments visible – preserving their documentary condition while deactivating their monumental power – can function as an open, everyday visual debate about the past and the futures it enables.

title: Imagineering the Future: A Mixed-Method Mapping of Japan’s Corporate Imaginaries of Metaverse Sustainability
abstract: Japanese metaverse discourse relies heavily on collective, often prescriptive visions of technoscientific futures. In general, these hyperbolic visions might be similar across the globe, but what about aspects they deliberately gloss over? Driven by this question, I examine Japan’s corporate metaverse discourse, focusing on the rarely thematized aspects of environmental and social sustainability. Based on Jasanoff’s concept of sociotechnical imaginaries, Adloff’s imaginaries of sustainability, and Brause et al.’s SIPC framework, my mixed-method approach identifies metaverse imaginaries through a combination of digital corpora analysis and semi-structured interviews with 14 expert practitioners from Japan. As a result, five sociotechnical imaginaries of sustainability emerge within Japan’s corporate metaverse discourse: anticipation, digital revolution, pragmatism, cultural essentialism, and technosolutionism. My analysis shows that the answers a nascent metaverse is expected to provide with regard to ecological and social crises depend on the type of metaverse we imagine and its relationship with the real world. The findings suggest that Japan’s imaginaries of metaverse sustainability are uniquely situated between an essentialized past, a challenging present, and distant futures, as well as between Japanese particularities and global tech ideologies.

title: Ambiguously queer: interrogating youth and queerness in Kyoto Animation’s adaptation of Sound! Euphonium
abstract: Found across a wide variety of genres, youth is a popular setting for media in Japan. Often focused on school club activities, narratives set during adolescence feature intense relationships between members of the same sex that toe the line between homoromantic and homosocial. The language used in the texts and by the creators often supports both readings, with the audience left to draw their own conclusions based on how they understand youth. While previous scholarship has looked at queerness in youth-focused texts, less has been written about how the association a text has with youth affects queer readings of the language of the texts. Through a textual and discourse analysis of the anime Sound! Euphonium (2015–2024), as well as published interviews with creators and online fan discussion about it, this article interrogates the relationship between queerness and youth in the Japanese media. I argue that youth has a normative effect in the Japanese media sphere, obfuscating the existence of queer readings by providing a normative explanation for even the queerest of language. I further suggest that Sound! Euphonium more widely reflects the ambiguity that pervades representations of queerness during female adolescence in the Japanese media.

title: The Right to Communicate: UNESCO and the politics of global communication, 1969–1987
abstract: Abstract The Right to Communicate (RtC) is the idea that individuals possess not only the freedom to ‘seek, receive and impart information’, as laid down in Article 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), but also the right to communicate horizontally with their peers, using technologies new and old. The brainchild of Jean d’Arcy, a French broadcaster and official who argued in 1969 that Article 19 should be updated to reflect the new technological possibilities, the concept inspired an international effort to write the RtC into human rights law. This article examines the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization’s (UNESCO) campaign to define this new human right, showing how initial enthusiasm was undermined by a widespread conviction that collective rights were a threat to individual rights; the difficulty of squaring the Global South’s state-led vision of communication with d’Arcy’s anti-statist ideals; and the vocal opposition of Western governments and NGOs, who increasingly saw the concept as a threat to freedom of information.

title: Knowledge uprooted: Transimperial forestry and the hiring of foreign experts in the Dutch East Indies, 1920s–1930s
abstract: Abstract This article examines the global networks underpinning colonial forestry in the Dutch East Indies in the interwar period. In the aftermath of the First World War, a renewed surge towards the internationalisation of the forest sciences served to open up imperial knowledge systems to a wider pool of outside expertise. This provided opportunities for smaller, thus far underresearched parties like the Nordic states, as explored here through a case study of a group of international foresters employed by the Dutch colonial administration in the 1930s. The article combines transimperial and global history approaches into a multisite analysis of both the scholarly exchanges that led to their initial hiring and their subsequent on-the-ground work in the colony. It is argued that an actor-oriented interrogation of the practical networks and internal frictions of colonial knowledge work reveals the hesitant emergence of a multilateral system that anticipated the post-1945 regime of international development.

title: The Futuristic Imagination Sprawl: Charting Concepts vs. Social Realities
abstract: This introductory article provides the theoretical framing for the Japanese Studies special issue, ‘Japanese Technofutures – Imaginaries, Narratives, Social Realities’. The contributions focus on Japan as a primary site for technofuturistic imaginations, driven by both external techno-orientalist attributions and deeply internalized self-conceptualizations. Yet, these technological promises frequently present a paradox: they commodify the future while masking persistent social and structural inequalities in the present. Acknowledging that both area studies and science and technology studies (STS) discursively construct their respective subjects, this introduction bridges the two fields by charting the conceptual landscape of the ‘futuristic imagination sprawl’. It demonstrates that differentiating Sheila Jasanoff’s sociotechnical imaginaries from adjacent concepts enriches our investigation of future-oriented imaginations with greater clarity and precision. Grounded in this framework, the special issue’s case studies examine how Japanese technofutures are envisioned, institutionalized, translated, and contested from the 1960s to the present.

title: ‘Floating Property’: Litigating Coastal Enclosure in Belfast’s Crown Court, 1886–1887
abstract: This article examines a case brought before the Belfast Spring Assizes in 1886 and again in 1887, in which three coastal smallholders from Ballycastle, County Antrim, were prosecuted for theft of seaweed from shores claimed by a local landlord. Drawing upon a variety of documents produced from the trial, this article examines how Irish legal institutions managed the indeterminate foreshore environment during a period of considerable land law reform. Central to this investigation is the consideration of how evidentiary hierarchies, upheld in court proceedings and enshrined in public judgements, informed public challenges to coastal enclosure. Written evidence bases (maps, leases, rent books) were privileged over oral testimony, with the effect of reinforcing absolutist, totalising visions of property ownership. Yet, through the hearing of oral testimonies, the courtroom retained a crucial function as a theatre for airing popular counterclaims. These depositions complicated the prosecution’s vision of coastal ownership, articulating the foreshore as a terraqueous environment governed by local custom and informal systems of exchange that were underpinned by understandings of reciprocity and common rights rather than exclusive title.

title: Luck Favors Those Who Show Merit
abstract: Abstract To manage the influx of diverse applicants and increase accountability, educational institutions have increasingly adopted high-stakes entrance exams. In response to intensified competition, recent US-based research suggests that growing belief in meritocracy leads “winners” to attribute success to hard work, feel morally superior to “losers,” and dismiss the role of luck. This study contributes to the broader understanding of the social-psychological impacts of meritocratic selection by drawing on qualitative longitudinal interviews with high school seniors at eighteen selective high schools in Japan, where college attendance is nearly universal. Follow-up interviews with graduates reveal that those who were not admitted to their first-choice universities tend to reject the idea that bad luck contributed to their failure, even though the admissions process contains unpredictable elements. Instead, they are more likely to attribute failure to insufficient effort—even in cases where their effort was substantial, and poor outcomes were largely due to chance. They then retrospectively rationalize their outcomes as appropriate or deserved. The article discusses the cultural and institutional factors that sustain strong support for effort-based meritocracy in Japan's high-stakes admissions system, and it considers the implications for inequality.

title: Why Bear the Burden of Student Loans?
abstract: Abstract This essay investigates what it means for young people in East Asia to go to college by looking at the growing number of young adults who attend higher education using National Student Loans. In-depth interviews with nineteen low-income young adults in South Korea and Japan revealed that the decision to attend college has become more common in both societies, with positive evaluations of National Student Loans and student debts. They strategically positioned their student loans by distinguishing them from other loans. In addition, the author found that higher education has more complex meanings in East Asia than simply a means of economic benefit. For example, in South Korea, higher education was equated with gaining prestige goods, while in Japan, going to college was considered the ideal way for young people to spend their twenties.

title: Representing Animals in Asian Screen Media: An Introduction
abstract: Abstract In Asia, the representation of animals serves as a narrative intermediary for contemplating the relationship between humans and nature. From ancient times to the present, Asian religions such as Buddhism and Japanese Shintoism have regarded animals as incarnations of deities. The mythical nature of animals is preserved in Asian screen media through adaptations based on ancient stories. In contemporary human life, animals have become production assets for labor, companions as pets, and content for digital platforms. The representation of animals not only reflects human life but also becomes critical of the ethics in the relationships between humans and animals in this late Anthropocene era. This special issue gathers scholars from across national borders to discuss how the representation of animals in East Asian screen media, including cinema, animation, gallery-based moving image, and short video platforms, differently reflects national culture, colonial history, and contemporary environmental and platform politics on screen.

title: The Contribution of Environmental History to Understanding Fires in Landscapes: Exploring Analogies between Case Studies in South Africa and Portugal
abstract: ABSTRACT This article offers comparative environmental histories of wildfires in Portugal and South Africa from c .1860 to the 2010s, using a framework derived from Elinor Ostrom’s work on managing communal environmental systems and an emerging integrated approach to wildfire management. In doing so, it sets out ideas for writing more systematic comparative historical analyses of wildfires while also using the case studies to show how historical analysis enriches case study approaches usually focused on natural and social science data and perspectives. It considers the particular versus the general, investigating whether historical analyses of fire use, management and occurrence can generate more holistic apprehensions of wildfire scenarios.

title: Burning the Black Dragon, Creating Dongbei: Fire Social Ecological History in Northeastern China, 1945–2005
abstract: ABSTRACT Modern China’s understanding of wildfires is primarily applied science aimed at resolving issues related to fire management. Dominant conceptions of fire focus on physical processes and interactions – a physical paradigm. This was not always the case and this historical survey and analysis of fires in northeast China (Dongbei) seeks to unpack a more biological and cultural wildfire paradigm based on key policy evolutions and wildfire events. Northeast China was transformed over the course of the twentieth century from mixed and boreal forest-grassland-wetland interface into one of the major ‘breadbaskets’ of China through migration, infrastructure and agricultural development, and extensive fire use and wildfire outbreaks. China’s understanding of fire, firefighting and fire policy evolved in tandem with this transformation, and increasing experience with major wildfire disasters in the region, leading to a more applied science and professionalised wildfire management approach. Based on historical analysis of settlement and landscape management trends, use of fire in land reclamation, together with evolving wildfire suppression and firefighting administrations in northeastern China, fostered a range of fire policy frameworks – from limited colonial regulation to socialist revolution and collectivisation approaches – and, overall, a total war on wildfire with varying success, through current wildfire management models.

title: The Burning Landscapes of the Serras of Southern Portugal: A Silent Transition from Fire-Centric Landscapes to Massive Forest Fires
abstract: ABSTRACT Over the course of the 1960s, the Monchique mountains in southern Portugal moved from a cereal-based rural economy to one based on eucalyptus trees channelled into the pulpwood industry. This swift change entailed the transition from a landscape mostly organised around fire farming practices to a forested landscape frequently devastated by large fires. This article proposes a long-term understanding of these changes and, more broadly, of the emergence of the current fire regime in the Portuguese mountains, focusing on the political, scientific, and ecological opposition between forest and fire that unfolded from the second half of the nineteenth century. Monchique shows, paradoxically, that rural fire use long resisted the ideal of a fire-free landscape until the birth of the recent massive forest fires.

title: Burning as a Throughline: A History of Anthropogenic Fires in the National Forests of North Carolina
abstract: ABSTRACT Anthropogenic fires constitute a throughline in the fire history of Nantahala and Pisgah National Forests of Western North Carolina; they have been used for different reasons by Indigenous and Settler communities, scientists and managers. Evidence from 8,000+ years of human presence in the region challenges hegemonic narratives in which a uniform, universal era of fire exclusion occurred. Prescribed burning has been promoted as one of the best practices for restoring safer fire regimes and healthier ecosystems. Fire managers have been working towards increasing prescribed burning operations within their jurisdictions. Rather than centring a clear suppression versus burning dichotomy or simplifying variability, this article enlists the concept of ‘culture’ to smooth out the transitions between times when human fires were absent and present, and connects twenty-first-century institutionalised fire management activities to previous people’s practices. Intentional burning has strong causal effects in contemporary managers’ and scientists’ paradigms, leading them to integrate fire into multipronged strategies for managing the Nantahala and Pisgah National Forests.

title: ‘Stinking Hot Weather’: Embodying Fire Suppression on the Ground and in the Air in Mid-Twentieth-Century British Columbia
abstract: ABSTRACT Histories of aerial firefighting in British Columbia [BC]’s Forest Service often frame the mid-twentieth century as a time of transformation from an agency of patrolmen fighting fires with hand tools to a technological system governed by enlightened professionals. The aeroplane was a convenient commemorative shorthand for a classic story of technological progress and success in fire suppression. In this article, we listen closely to the oral histories of two forest rangers working on the fire line during the introduction of aerial fire suppression technologies in the mid-twentieth century. By analysing these interviews and related archival materials, we contribute to embodied and sensory histories of colonial fire suppression practices in BC and work to situate them in their specific institutional, social and cultural contexts. Close attention to the sensory experience of firefighting men shows how embodied, individual and situated knowledge shaped the work of fire control in the BC Forest Service.

title: Ministerial Power in Kantei-Led Policymaking: The Case of the Priority Reform Promotion System for National Universities under the Second Abe Administration
abstract: This article examines the policymaking process of the Priority Reform Promotion System, a performance-based funding system for Japanese national universities introduced under the second Abe administration. Existing research has largely portrayed this process through the lens of Kantei-led (prime minister’s office-led) policymaking, which sees the Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT) as following directives set by prime ministerial councils. However, little attention has been paid to whether and how MEXT’s own preferences were incorporated into the policy design. Using policy documents and elite interviews with MEXT civil servants, this article traces the policymaking process from agenda setting to the final budget negotiations, taking seriously the agency of MEXT. The findings show that MEXT held clear preferences from an early stage and shaped the design of the system within the new Kantei-led structure. These findings indicate that the Kantei-led framework does not on its own explain who determines specific policy content and suggest that ministerial agency deserves closer attention in analyses of Japan’s centralised policymaking structure.

title: Environment, Infrastructure and Epidemics in Late Ottoman Bursa: A Perspective from Environmental History
abstract: Examining epidemic diseases from the perspective of environmental history demonstrates that epidemics were not merely the result of biological processes, but were produced within socio-ecological interactions shaped by water infrastructures, industrial production, waste regimes, animal mobility and rural–urban circulation. By centring the concepts of environmental memory (continuity or rupture between past, present and future) and infrastructural inertia (inaction, stagnation, immutability and consequently deterioration and obsolescence), this study reveals that, despite administrative reforms, the risks associated with epidemics persisted through the material environment and deeply entrenched infrastructures. Through the case of Bursa, this article argues that epidemics cannot be understood independently from their environmental and infrastructural contexts. Archival documents and sanitary reports demonstrate that the structural deterioration of Bursa’s water distribution systems, the organic waste generated by silk production, the role of animal markets in zoonotic circulation and rural–urban mobility collectively shaped epidemic dynamics. Although modern public health measures such as quarantine and cordon practices were implemented, contaminated water flows, production-based waste, uncontrolled animal movements and livelihood-driven compulsory mobility limited the effectiveness of these measures. title: Who cares about Otto? The monument of Otto von Bismarck in Bielefeld between commemoration, forgetting, and intervention
abstract: Monuments remain physically present long after the commemorative practices and shared interpretations that once sustained them have eroded. This article examines this process through the history of the Bismarck monument in Bielefeld, Germany, from its inauguration in 1903 to the present. Drawing on archival sources, newspaper reports, city council records, and documentation of recent interventions, it traces three successive memory regimes: national-heroic commemoration, postwar historicization and spatial marginalization, and the contemporary pluralization of meaning. It shows that political ruptures do not necessarily coincide with mnemonic change and that forgetting often unfolds gradually through shifting practices, spatial contexts, and communities of memory. Treating forgetting not as erasure but as a constitutive operation of memory, the article argues that the erosion of established meanings creates the conditions for new and competing historical appropriations.

title: A Technological and Ecological Tangle: Growers, Insects and Pesticides in Norwegian Horticulture, 1945–1960
abstract: The springboard for this article is a student diary from a Norwegian horticultural college in 1950. The notebook provides insights on how to use chemical insecticides, or in other words, poisons. The student kept day-to-day notes on what he was taught, and what he practised in the greenhouses and out in the fields and orchards. Alongside his fellow students in post-war Norway, he was taught to use toxic substances to ‘manage’ elements in nature. The diary is a snapshot of pesticide practices at that horticultural college from March to October 1950. After World War Two, efforts in horticulture to cultivate and control non-human nature, such as insects, intensified as new technologies such as industrial machines and different chemicals became readily available, firmly advocated and widely applied. These technologies facilitated changes on a scale previously unseen in human history. This article explores how new pesticide technologies affected the interaction between growers, plants and insects in Norwegian horticulture between 1945 and 1960. The investigation is based on the horticultural student diary from 1950 together with recently conducted oral history interviews from horticulturists who practised from the late 1940s onwards.

title: The Shifting Narrative of a Scottish Sandstorm in Time
abstract: This work explores the shifting narrative of the Culbin disaster, a series of storm events in 1694 that caused severe damage to a local community, with attention to the changes of that narrative over time. It highlights several major themes including how the human element of Culbin, despite being documented in the first accounts of the events, has come and gone from the narrative, the emphasis on the storm itself, the spiritual element of early modern disasters, the power of nature, Culbin as a symbol of triumph, and anxieties of climate change. Culbin serves as a long-term study of a disaster and explores how people chose to remember it.

title: Poetics as historical methodology
abstract: How can the tools of the poet enrich the writing of history? Some of history refuses translation. The past leaves gaping gestures in its records, for the historian to evade, or gloss over, or critically fabulate, as it leaves sediments of fractured story, layered through the processes of historical production. How can the historian attune to, and then amend, these formal contours of the archive? I argue that poetics can place the possibility and impossibility of recovering violent or entangled archives into the form of history-writing. I call for a re-envisioning of our forms of historical narration which draws from (or ‘Slants’) the poetics of the archive. Learning from four poets who embed the archive’s contours into the forms of their poetics, and from my own experiences writing archival poetry, I craft a poetics of history-telling that bares the seams of the historical process and holds those rhythms of the archive otherwise lost to historical prose. How completely can we embed the archive’s modes of memory-making into the form of our narratives? I turn to poetics as a new historical method.

title: BCOF at eighty: new perspectives on the British commonwealth occupation force in the occupation of Japan
abstract: The British Commonwealth Occupation Force (BCOF) component of the Allied Occupation of Japan (1945-1952) has often been overlooked by researchers because of its minimal role in policy-making. Taking the opportunity of the 80th anniversary of the arrival of the first BCOF personnel in Japan, this special issue introduces new perspectives about the organisation based on a range of hitherto unused or under-utilised sources. The introduction begins by emphasising how BCOF’s commanding officer sought to draw attention to his troops’ contribution to the Occupation. There follows a brief overview of the existing secondary research about BCOF in English and in Japanese. The latter half of the introduction outlines the contribution that the four articles make to the special issue. Taken as a whole, the purpose of the special issue is to begin to reassess how the occupiers and the occupied understood the role and meaning of BCOF. The introduction concludes with a call for other researchers to take part in the process of making this reassessment.

title: II. Chronologies
abstract: Abstract Despite a recent shift towards Global South-centred histories of development, women in and from Asia and Africa remain largely neglected in the historiography. In response, this Arenas issue examines the implications of situating the roles and experiences of women at the centre of historical analysis in this field. Bringing together scholars with diverse research expertise, the discussion reflects on the gendered meanings of development in twentieth-century colonial and post-colonial societies and emphasises the need for an expansive definition that takes in social welfare activities alongside industrial and economic projects. The forum explores some of the ways in which researching Asian and African women’s histories of development present particular challenges while at the same time offering conceptual and methodological insights that are relevant to the wider field. ‘Chronologies’ considers the question of periodisation and offers nuanced correctives to established narratives of continuity and rupture in the historiography of development.

title: Addressing AI-generated disinformation in Japan: challenges, limitations, and prospective policy directions
abstract: This study examines Japan’s challenges and approaches to AI-generated disinformation, identified by the World Economic Forum as one of the top short-term global risks for 2026. By presenting specific cases and dissemination channels, it discusses the circulation of such content and highlights the serious threats it poses to the public. The study further explores potential contextual factors that may contribute to the spread of AI-generated disinformation in Japan, including possible collectivistic and uncertainty-avoidance characteristics of Japanese society, challenges in critically evaluating information, the gradual decline in trust in traditional media alongside the increasing use of social networking services, and comparatively low levels of institutional trust. The study then analyses Japan’s existing legal, policy, and technological countermeasures against AI-generated disinformation, emphasising weaknesses, challenges, and areas for improvement. Based on the findings, it proposes specific policy directions for developing more robust future responses and highlights the importance of adopting a more proactive approach that complements existing research-based and reactive strategies to strengthen societal resilience.

title: Unshackled?: China, the ‘unequal treaties’, and the limits of international law, 1919–1929
abstract: Abstract The post-1919 international order extended to China formal sovereign equality while offering few legal means to exercise it. The Sino-Belgian treaty dispute of 1926–29 reveals this: when China abrogated its 1865 treaty with Belgium and Brussels sued at the Permanent Court of International Justice, the institutions that promised peaceful revision could not deliver it without the consent of the powers whose privileges were at stake. The ‘unequal treaties’, a political category coined only in 1923, named the contradiction the order had built in. Four lawyer-diplomats—Wellington Koo, Wang Chung-hui, C.T. Wang, and Eugene Chen—were each caught between national autonomy and admission among the ‘civilised’ powers. The turn from legal argument to ‘revolutionary diplomacy’ was the structure’s doing, not a failure of nerve. Read beside Turkey, Persia, and the Latin American states, China’s case locates the obstacle: not semi-peripheral weakness as such, but the institutional position from which each engaged an order that subordinated its members through the very terms of their admission.

title: Humanitarianism, race, and the late colonial global order: Red Cross prison inspections in Apartheid South Africa
abstract: Abstract This article interrogates the politics of global humanitarianism and its entanglement with racial oppression during Africa’s decolonization by examining the International Committee of the Red Cross’s (ICRC) first prison visits to Apartheid South Africa in the 1960s. Using newly available archives from liberation movements, anti-Apartheid collections, the Apartheid state, and the ICRC itself, it shows how a global humanitarian organization was appropriated as a legitimating façade in the governance of a late colonial global order. Rather than scrutinizing Apartheid policies or safeguarding prisoners of colour, the ICRC’s prison visits reframed collaboration as humanitarian neutrality, thereby enabling White minority rule. Afro-Asian critics, however, articulated alternative legal and humanitarian visions that challenged the Red Cross’s claims to impartiality, neutrality, and universality. The article unsettles triumphalist accounts that portray Red Cross humanitarianism as neutral, leading, and/or inherently progressive, and instead emphasizes its structural incorporation into Apartheid’s political order. In doing so, it contributes to a global history of humanitarianism and international organizations that calls for a more critical reckoning with how international organizations instrumentalize and memorialize their pasts.

title: Blind spots: how death became visible in late Ottoman Istanbul, 1870–1900
abstract: Biological death did not automatically acquire perceptual, epistemic, or administrative legibility in late Ottoman Istanbul. Drawing on Ottoman archival records and contemporary press reports, this article examines how concealed, decomposed, fragmented, and otherwise indeterminate human remains entered regimes of recognition, identification, and official intervention. I use the term governed invisibility to describe how historically produced spatial, sensory, material, and institutional arrangements conditioned the perceptibility and administrative handling of human remains without deliberate concealment. Smell, decomposition, accidental exposure, and infrastructural disruption precipitated discovery, while police intervention, medical examination, personal objects, documentary traces, and forensic procedures recast bodily remains as objects of identification and evidentiary interpretation. Whereas existing scholarship has followed death from notification and examination through certification and registration, this article reconstructs the unstable threshold preceding those processes, tracing an uneven passage from disappearance to perceptible presence, from presence to a recognizable body, and from the body to administrative and forensic evidence.

title: The distorted Catholicism in Yokomitsu Riichi’s Ryoshū ( a traveller’s sadness ): a critical analysis of Western ideological implications as scientised religion
abstract: This study argues that the Catholicism depicted in Yokomitsu Riichi’s Ryoshū is not a reflection of its original mystical essence, but a rationalised and de-spiritualised Western construct imported into Japan. Through a close analysis of Yashiro, the novel’s protagonist, the paper explores how this form of Catholicism becomes a symbol of epistemic domination and cultural dissonance. Contrasting sharply with the aesthetic and nature-based spirituality of Ko-Shintō, the imported faith reflects a broader ideological intrusion. Yashiro’s rejection of Western religious logic and embrace of Eastern mystical epistemology represents an intellectual resistance to cultural homogenisation. Ryoshū thus dramatises Japan’s struggle to preserve metaphysical plurality and spiritual identity in the face of Western imperial influence. The psychological collapse of characters caught between conflicting worldviews further illustrates the deep cultural and existential tensions at play. Ultimately, the novel becomes a critical site for reimagining national identity and reclaiming epistemological autonomy.

title: The Cultural Revolution—CR/10—Project at the University of Pittsburgh
abstract: The Cultural Revolution—CR/10 Project is an oral history initiative launched in 2016 by the East Asian Library at the University of Pittsburgh Library System. Conceived to mark the fiftieth anniversary of the Cultural Revolution (1966–1976), the project responds to a critical gap in the historical record: while secondary literature and elite memoirs abound, systematically collected first-person accounts from ordinary individuals remain scarce. CR/10 addresses this imbalance by documenting the lived experiences of people who directly or indirectly experienced the movement, including members of the post–Cultural Revolution generation. Each video interview opens with three baseline questions, then turning to openended reflection, and runs a classroom-friendly ten to thirty minutes with English subtitles. Using snowball sampling, the project has gathered more than 120 interviews from participants across the United States, mainland China, Japan, and Europe, presented through a searchable website and interactive map. Beyond preservation, CR/10 has become a widely adopted teaching tool that shows students “history is complicated” and equips them to resist oversimplification. As a librarian-initiated effort to create rather than merely collect primary sources, CR/10 models an evolving role for research libraries in the digital age.

title: (Mis)managing Finances on a Global Scale: The Accounting Documents of the Jesuit Mission to Japan
abstract: Abstract This article aims at describing the sixteenth-seventeenth century Jesuit Japan mission’s finances through its accounting documents. The article demonstrates that accounting documents played a key role in the dialogue with Rome over the mission’s financial management and needs. Portraying a mission dependent on Europe and India to secure its resources, the accounts raise the question of how religious orders managed funds on a global scale. This article provides a detailed analysis of a type of source specific to the Society of Jesus, namely its catalogues. While it was common for overseas missions to purchase goods from Europe or other distant places, the Japan mission was singular in that it also had highly dispersed sources of income, spreading between Europe and Asia. This article demonstrates how the Jesuits of Japan articulated these resources and their disbursements, so that they could meet the material and spiritual needs of their evangelical project. The study of the catalogues thus reveals the challenges faced by a mission trying to manage its finances between Europe and Asia. It questions the order’s ability to design and enforce an administrative and institutional framework that could fit the complex case of globally deployed religious missions.

title: Onlife remembrance: the case of the 1993 Sivas Massacre
abstract: The increasing entanglement of online and offline memory environments has transformed the ways in which the past is remembered, remediated, and represented in our hyper-connected era. Various existing approaches, however, continue to treat online and offline dimensions of memory as distinct, overlooking their entanglement in contemporary remembrance practices. This article addresses this conceptual and methodological gap by critically engaging with the limitations of such approaches and theorizing onlife remembrance as an analytical framework for rethinking the multifaceted acts and experiences of remembrance of the historical past that emerge through the intra-actions of online and offline contexts within the interconnected nodes of the global infosphere. To demonstrate the explanatory potential of this framework in practice, the article offers a detailed case analysis of onlife remembrance of the 1993 Sivas/Madımak Massacre in Turkey, examining users’ mnemonic engagements with audiovisual remediations of the massacre on YouTube alongside user interactions within the 3D immersive environment of the Virtual Madımak Massacre Museum.

title: Between disconnection and connection: The paradoxes of Cold War export controls
abstract: Abstract This article reinterprets Cold War multilateral export controls not simply as mechanisms restricting access to strategic technologies, but as sites of mediated connection within Cold War globalisation. Moving beyond a US-centred framework, it examines West Germany’s experience of the China embargo under ChinCom in the 1950s and the liberalisation of controls in respect of China within CoCom in the 1980s. It asks how regimes designed to enforce technological disconnection generated new forms of global connectivity, arguing that this transformation can be understood through Western alliance asymmetries and CoCom’s role as an institutionalised site of transit. In the 1950s, embargo enforcement produced alternative re-export routes and unintended transnational connections. In the 1980s, competitive alliance manoeuvring revealed CoCom’s regulatory architecture as a space of negotiation where technological circulation was enabled, delayed, redirected, or politically obscured. A case study of Messerschmitt-Bölkow-Blohm illustrates how these dynamics operated in practice. By tracing mediated technological circulation across different phases of controls in respect of China, the article reframes Cold War globalisation as shaped by dis:connectivity: the mutually constitutive interplay of connection and disconnection.

title: From page to place: the tourist gaze at hot springs in Mayu kakushi no rei
abstract: In this article, I analyse the setting of Narai in Mayu kakushi no rei (1924) by Izumi Kyōka to show how literary representations and tourist practices interact to produce the cultural space of hot springs in modern Japan. I argue that the journey of the protagonist is mediated through guidebooks and novels that influence how he sees the place, making travel a compromise between familiar images and new experiences. At the same time, the failed attempt to build a hot-spring resort results in a mix of new structures and old architecture, creating an uncertain space that loosens social norms to invite mystery and melodrama. This uncertain space also lets the supernatural appear hand in hand with an eerie sensuality conveyed through sound and smell. Overall, most of these themes belong to a repertoire established in previous texts like Konjiki yasha (1897–1903), Hototogisu (1898–1899) and Kusamakura (1906), which had already associated hot springs with specific patterns of imagination and consumption. By looking at Mayu kakushi no rei in this genealogy, I show how representations of hot springs participated in the discourses that shaped the tourist gaze in modern Japan.

title: Japan’s plain language activities – from simplification of official texts to Yasashii nihongo
abstract: This article examines Japan’s three approaches to language simplification—Plain Japanese, the simplification of official documents, and Yasashii nihongo (Easy/Kind Japanese)—and situates them within international plain‑ and easy‑language frameworks. Although Japan lacks a unified national policy, these strands emerged in different institutional contexts: internationally oriented plain‑language activities, domestic administrative reforms, and the educationally anchored development of Yasashii nihongo for multicultural coexistence. Drawing on Japanese and international scholarship, governmental guidelines, and historical sources, the article traces the development and aims of each initiative and identifies challenges, including tensions between inclusion and gatekeeping, the reproduction of ‘us/them’ boundaries, and limited theoretical grounding. The article provides the first comprehensive English‑language overview of Japan’s plain/easy‑language landscape and argues for integrating Japanese practices more systematically into global research on linguistic accessibility.

title: Ethics in history: introducing conceptual tools for research practices
abstract: The article argues that historical research is an inherently ethical endeavor: It intervenes in contemporary society by engendering new understandings of its past, thus affecting individual and collective imaginaries of society’s current situation and possible futures. This calls for ethical considerations at every step in the research process, from the identification of a topic to the production and dissemination of a historical narrative. While many historians have engaged with ethical questions, conceptual tools for analyzing ethical problems pertaining to research practices and knowledge interventions are lacking. Building on the work of Michel-Rolph Trouillot and Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick, the article suggests two continua – visibility/invisibility and critical/enabling – that scholars might employ to map and reflect on the ethical implications of their research. The final part presents an example from current scholarship to illustrate how the tools can be used to think through the plethora of ethically fraught choices that historians encounter while formulating research questions, developing methodologies, selecting sources, coining analytical concepts and constructing arguments.

title: Making a Nuclear Possibility Space: Exploratory Gas Centrifuge Research in Postwar Japan
abstract: This article examines the early history of gas centrifuge research in postwar Japan, focusing on how and why exploratory uranium enrichment research emerged and persisted despite the absence of a clearly articulated national policy. Drawing on primary sources and contemporary publications, it analyzes gas centrifuge research at the Institute of Physical and Chemical Research (RIKEN) between 1959 and 1962, led by chemical engineer Yoshitoshi Oyama. The article argues that Japan’s early engagement with centrifuge technology cannot be explained solely by the international diffusion of knowledge. Instead, it was shaped by the interaction of the US-led regime of nuclear knowledge control, the institutionalized norm against military use of nuclear energy, and institutional arrangements for peaceful nuclear development. Within this constrained environment, Oyama initiated small-scale experimental research that avoided both military associations and premature industrial commitments. Although limited in scope, RIKEN’s centrifuge project laid technical and institutional foundations that later facilitated the incorporation of uranium enrichment into Japan’s nuclear development program. By tracing the emergence and institutionalization of this exploratory research, the article contributes to scholarship on Japan’s nuclear history and illustrates how research on sensitive technologies can be pursued within a historically constructed space of political, normative, and institutional …

title: Fraught Narratives, Contrived Futures: Tokyo’s Techno-Utopian Erasure of the Unhoused
abstract: Mirai – future – is ubiquitously written into Tokyo’s cityscape. Yet the promises embedded in future-oriented government initiatives like Health Japan 21, Innovation 25, Society 5.0, and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), reveal a growing disconnect between techno-utopian visions and lived realities. Here I explore this tension by examining how advocacy organizations for Tokyo’s unhoused provide a more humane, dignity-oriented future, challenging the consumerist and techno-utopian solutions offered by official initiatives. Through ethnographic fieldwork with Nojiren, Tenohasi, and Sanyukai – groups aiding Tokyo’s unhoused – I contrast grassroots efforts with government-driven narratives that promote an idealized ‘future past’, where nostalgia and promises of technological progress serve as a weakening panacea for social and economic concerns. These top-down efforts, designed to reassure an aging population facing economic uncertainty, often obscure the immediate struggles many face. By highlighting the work of advocacy groups, I argue that smaller-scale, community-driven efforts offer a more inclusive, emancipatory, and compassionate path forward.

title: An Interspecies Contact Zone: Locusts and Humans in Colonial Burundi, 1929–1941
abstract: In interwar Burundi, successive waves of gregarious locust swarms preyed on fields and grazing grounds, exacerbating the vulnerability of its (non)-human inhabitants. The locusts also constituted an acute governance issue for the Belgian colonial administration, which struggled to devise efficient modes of acridian destruction. By using locust being-in-the-world as a vantage point, this article analyses the complex interactions between insectile hazards and the segregated human communities who had to face them. It delves into the differing perspectives of Burundian peasants and colonial administrators, and looks at the connected modes of containment that emerged across the colonial divide. On a conceptual level, the article proposes the concept ‘interspecies contact zone’ as a framework to make sense of more-than-human encounters occurring in the fraught context of colonial societies. title: Daughters of the First Empire: Inherited wealth, surveillance, and Napoleon’s contested imperial power
abstract: Abstract Young daughters occupy an anomalous position in the legal landscape of Napoleonic France. While the Civil Code of 1804 reduced wives to legal dependents, it guaranteed daughters equal inheritance rights alongside their brothers, a striking exception within an otherwise conservative family law. This article suggests that the anomaly was not incidental: rather than reflecting principled commitment, Napoleon’s retention of egalitarian inheritance may have derived from his recognition that a growing market of wealthy heiresses could serve as instruments of political consolidation. By orchestrating marriages between these women and loyal officers, his government hoped to fuse old noble families with the new imperial notables. To identify suitable candidates, Savary, the minister of police, secretly ordered prefects to compile detailed lists on young women across the empire. Two surviving tables, from the departments of Vienne and the annexed Simplon (today Valais, Switzerland), illustrate how this project unfolded on the ground, and why it largely failed. Though Napoleon’s matchmaking schemes yielded meagre results, the tables themselves document a significant moment in the history of state bureaucratic science and surveillance: the incorporation of young women’s bodies, fortunes, and futures into the administrative machinery of imperial power.

title: Everyday Bureaucratic Authoritarianism under South African Apartheid
abstract: The standard by which the police operate is cruelly simple: every black man is a criminal suspect. In a technical sense, the police are not far off the mark to be so suspicious. The laws of apartheid are a far-reaching tangle of restrictions, reaching so deeply into everyday life that it is a rare African who does not violate some law. A policeman may at any time call upon any African who is sixteen or older to produce his reference book. If the African fails to produce it, or if his papers are not in order, he is committing a criminal offence and is liable to a fine or imprisonment. This is the nub of the infamous “pass laws,” a complex mesh of rules and regulations that restrict the freedom of movement of Africans. Compared to some of the other oppressive statutes of apartheid, the pass laws on paper seem modest enough. But in practice they are the keynote on which enforcement of the entire apartheid system is based.

title: On Memory and Morphology: Field Notes from Tokyo’s Arboreal Archive of Wartime Destruction
abstract: This source note introduces a rich and largely unknown archive of Tokyo’s long history of urban conflagration: sensai jumoku, the scores of trees scattered across the city that carry the scars of wartime firebombing in their morphology. It profiles five particular war-damaged trees, each offering different insights into the interpretative challenges and opportunities that come with working in this arboreal archive of destruction. Far from static witnesses to the past, these shape-shifting trees tell remarkable stories not only of war and defeat but also of care and repair. At a time when memories of World War II are rapidly fading and catastrophic fire disasters are growing more frequent, the task of conveying these stories is more urgent than ever.

title: Mandarin of the Ecological Modern: Hassan Fathy, Nature, and the Postcolonial African City
abstract: In the early 1960s, the Egyptian architect Hassan Fathy traveled throughout West Africa as part of the City of the Future (COF) research project, which aimed to collect data on urban life across the world. This essay examines Fathy’s writings about postcolonial Africa as part of the COF project. It suggests that this work set him apart from a broader consensus among technocratic elites and postcolonial political leaders about the human relationship with the natural world that emphasized an imperative to manage, control, and direct. Instead, Fathy sought to synthesize his long-standing interests in climate, architecture, and urbanism with the question of decolonization on the African continent and concluded that a postcolonial approach to urban architecture and design necessitated a return to precolonial methods of construction and planning, ones embedded in and responsive to city’s ecological contexts.

title: The Transition to Wage Labour, in Stone, in North Wales, in Jamaica
abstract: Abstract Completed around 1821, a monument commemorating the enslaver and industrialist Richard Pennant and his wife, Anne Susannah Warburton, elides any mention of the family’s sugar plantations in Jamaica and instead celebrates the Pennants as benevolent modernizers who transformed their Welsh estate and tenants. A material artefact of national history writing, the monument severs this local story from imperial concerns. Yet a comparative study of the transition to wage labour on the family’s properties in North Wales and Jamaica reveals the work the Pennant memorial’s story was doing for both Britain’s local and its imperial labour projects. In North Wales, estate managers confronted labourers’ independence; in post-emancipation Jamaica, plantation authorities similarly faced freed people’s efforts to defend their autonomy. Racial ideology reconciled these parallel histories by constructing Black labourers as uniquely idle, thereby legitimizing restrictive post-emancipation labour regimes while masking coercion within Britain itself. By tracing the circulation of labour ideologies, moral vocabularies, and managerial practices across North Wales and Jamaica, this article challenges historical narratives that separate industrial Britain from slave and post-slave colonies, a tendency epitomized in the Pennant monument, and instead exposes the joint construction of national mythology and imperial rationality.

title: The ghost of Butterfield and the writing of UK official nuclear history
abstract: In a major critical article about UK official history written in 1949, Herbert Butterfield, highlighted what he viewed as the inherent weaknesses of government-sponsored history and argued that all such histories should be subjected to ‘unremitting scrutiny’. Despite the resurgence of interest in analysing the wide range of UK official histories in recent years one important subject has been neglected: UK policy on nuclear weapons. This article seeks to remedy this gap in the historiography of UK official history by focusing attention on the work of the three main official nuclear historians. A number of key questions are considered: are the official nuclear histories simply attempts by governments to ‘control the past’?; are they ‘honest’ histories, reflecting the highest professional standards?; did the historians have unimpeded access to all the documents?; were the historians ‘institutionalized’?; and are there significant gaps in their coverage of important areas of nuclear policy? The article argues that while they provide significant and important contributions to knowledge, not available to those without privileged access, these histories do require cautious, constant scrutiny and challenge. Even with such scrutiny, however, it is argued that they should be regarded as ‘foundational’ studies.

title: Secret Hitler and the ghosts of Weimar: a ludic case study in ‘Hitlersploitation’?
abstract: Juxtaposing recent advances in Historical Game Studies with historical research on the commercialisation of the Third Reich in contemporary culture, this article treats the board game Secret Hitler (2016) as a case study in ‘Hitlersploitation’. It argues that analysing this popular social deduction game and its fraught reception in depth can shed light on highly significant historical themes, including Western cultural obsessions with Nazism; the use of ‘Weimar analogies’ to frame the threat of fascism in the present day, and the ways in which cultures around games and gaming can have an impact on politicised memory cultures (and vice versa). Contrasting the game’s emplotment of the fall of the Weimar Republic with more recent historiographical approaches to this period, we can also interpret Secret Hitler and the discourse surrounding it as a manifestation of what Daniel Bessner has termed the ‘Ghosts of Weimar’ – highlighting the ‘doomed’ Republic’s capacity to haunt us in the present. Finally, the article argues that not only digital games, but also modern analogue games – even those of an ostensibly trivial or ‘light-weight’ nature – need to be taken seriously as cultural artefacts of potential historical and historiographical importance.

title: Gandhi’s Voice, Mass Politics, and the Arrival of Public Address Technology in India, 1927–1931
abstract: Abstract Historians often draw on texts of public speeches in an effort to understand the politics of the past, while seldom pausing to consider if they were audible at the time. This is particularly relevant to the case of anti-colonialism in South Asia between the two world wars, when political speeches were typically delivered to mass open-air audiences and audibility must have been a considerable challenge. Historians have assumed that the arrival of public address systems in India overcame this problem, but a focus on the phase of its implementation, as both speakers and audiences gradually became acculturated to the ways in which microphones and loudspeakers mediated public speaking, shows how unreliable they were, introducing new dynamics and challenges to the processes of both speaking and listening. Adopting an intermedial, multisensory approach and focusing on speeches by M. K. Gandhi, who sought to dominate inter-war anti-colonialism in British India, this article looks for ways of understanding how political messaging operated in contexts where being able to hear a speech was not a given.

title: Nonhuman as Mediation: Agency of Nonhuman Animals in Miyazaki’s Animation
abstract: Abstract Hayao Miyazaki’s animated films have long been characterized by animistic ideas and ecological thought. In his works, nonhuman characters, including nonhuman animals and machines, mediate relationships among humans, society, and the natural world. During World War II , nonhuman animal characters served as key instruments of political propaganda and national identity in both American and Japanese animated films, and this tradition has persisted in contemporary Japanese animated films. However, such representations have gradually shifted from speciesism to cultural representations that serve contemporary film narratives. This article takes Hayao Miyazaki’s The Boy and the Heron (2023) as a case study to analyze how nonhuman animal figures generate agency through the narrative process and to propose the concept of “animal-imagery species” to explore the mediating role of nonhuman beings in Japanese animated films.

title: The Nuclear Beautiful : The Ethics and Aesthetics of the Bomb in the Writings of Mishima Yukio
abstract: Following seminal critical work by Frances Ferguson (1984) and Peter B. Hales (1991), many writers have invoked the aesthetic category of the sublime when describing artists' and observers' responses to nuclear weapons; the technical term has thus been the nuclear sublime. This article argues for the viability of a related but different aesthetic category: the nuclear beautiful. Twentieth-century creators working in various media represented a seemingly improbable aesthetic response to nuclear explosions: under certain circumstances, a spectator might find beauty in a nuclear detonation and its effects. Mishima Yukio's novel Utsukushii hoshi (Beautiful Star, 1962) and other writings explore the ethical implications of finding beauty in the destructive power of nuclear weapons. Because of certain aspects of the narrative construction of Beautiful Star, however, the question of the ethicality of the nuclear beautiful is left unresolved, as the novel incisively probes a variety of responses to the threat of global nuclear annihilation.

title: Competing with Housewives on the Home Front : Kyoto's Geisha and the Fifteen Years' War
abstract: This article examines the role imposed on and adopted by Kyoto's geisha during wartime, and analyzes the complex situation in which geisha assumed the appearance of housewives, suppressed their own identity, and actively cooperated with the war effort. The Women's National Defense Association, established in Osaka in 1932, sought to engage women from geisha districts. When the Kyoto Headquarters opened in 1934, geisha also participated, and each district formed its own branch. The Association's branch in Gion Kōbu, the renowned geisha district in Kyoto, eventually contributed three airplanes to the army and navy. The military, local governments, and the women's associations themselves all orchestrated competition to support the war effort. Media coverage of the fundraising campaigns and their contributors further fueled this competition, amplifying the success of the campaign. This article argues that geisha were participants in this competition, and through their activities sought to showcase their significant contribution to the war effort. The identity these geisha adopted took on elements associated with domesticity—most notably, the attire of housewives—despite geisha being seen as the antithesis of the domestic housewife. The situation of the geisha illustrates the challenges of establishing identity in a patriarchal society where women were expected to remain invisible beyond the domestic sphere.

title: Ginkei and Co. : Commodifying Literati Identity in Nineteenth-Century Japan
abstract: This article examines commercial publications by Hata Ginkei and his associates to understand how they used the labels of "literati" (bunjin) and "masters" (sensei) as advertisements. Combining literary analysis and historical contextualization, I argue that an emerging group of amateur cultural practitioners did not rely solely on selling, writing, and painting to make a living. They used their social connections and wealth to seek recognition in commercial publications through exchanges of cash and favors. Ginkei and his associates commodified literary identity in order to produce fictional rankings and compilations of calligraphy and painting. This led to an expanded group of "literati" in the mid-nineteenth century. However, by turning the identity of literatus into a title that amateurs could buy and authors could sell, Ginkei and Co. obscured the value of the cultural practices with which this identity had previously been associated.

title: Plants in the Shade : Cryptogams as Queer Metaphor in Modern Japanese Discourse
abstract: The now-archaic botanical term "cryptogam" was used to refer to ferns, mushrooms, and other plants thought to reproduce without producing seeds. In Japanese, however, the term cryptogam (inka shokubutsu) has been used as a metaphor for queer sexualities since shortly after World War II. Starting in the early 1950s, inka shokubutsu began to be used to refer to queer communities emerging in Tokyo and other urban centers and was subsequently adopted by mainstream media during the 1960s and 1970s. By the 1990s, however, the term had fallen out of use, as a new generation of LGBTQ activists argued that it had discriminatory connotations. This article shows how cryptogams emerged as a unique metaphor for queerness in Japanese literature and media over the course of the twentieth century and argues that debates over the term's meaning illuminate larger questions of queer representation and visibility in contemporary Japan.
