title: Kyoto's Universities at War, 1937-1945 : Using Institutional History, Addressing Institutional Responsibility
abstract: The development of Japan's university sector was a key factor in Japan's modernization process after the Meiji Restoration. The period from the 1870s to 1940s was also a period of Japanese imperialism, and from the 1930s, militarism. As a result, many of Japan's oldest and most prestigious universities, both national/public and private, made important scientific, social, and intellectual contributions to imperialism and militarism. This article examines how three prestigious universities in Kyoto—Kyoto University, Ritsumeikan University, and Doshisha University—have presented their wartime roles in university histories. These universities—a national (formerly imperial) university, a private secular university, and a private religious university, respectively—constitute a useful microcosm of the broader higher education sector in the 1930s. Furthermore, Kyoto's relative lack of wartime destruction during air raids forces the universities to focus on their active roles in the war effort rather than passive victimhood. The article analyzes the universities' histories as presented in university websites, official university histories, on-campus exhibitions, and the research of individual academics and employees. It demonstrates how a university produces multiple versions of its own history, presenting quite different images of its past. Understanding these differences requires identifying the actors within the university who produced the history, for what purpose, and how they …

title: Materiality, Visuality, and Phenomenology : Strategies of Reproduction in Modern Japanese Books
abstract: This research note investigates competing strategies of reproduction employed in modern Japanese books with reference to three specific volumes. The first is the Overview of Useful Lumber (Yūyō mokuzai shōran) published in 1874; the second is an early chromolithographic publication, the Chōyōkaku Appreciations: Brocades Section (Chōyōkaku kanshō, kinshū no bu) of 1883; and the third is a deluxe facsimile of an early-modern album of treasured calligraphy known as the Verdure tekagami (Tekagami nobe no midori) from 1972. Each publication evokes the issue of sampling: tranches of wood in Useful Lumber, chromolithography in Brocades, and full-scale facsimiles in the Verdure tekagami. The research note examines changing investments in remediation across this hundred-year span while foregrounding the issue of phenomenological preservation—the way in which reproductions, copies, and facsimiles work to preserve not just the appearance but the experience of the original.

title: Imperial Household Grants from 1914 to 1945 : On the Social Functions of the Monarchy in Modern Japan
abstract: In this article, I analyze the social function of the monarchy in modern Japan by examining disbursements of grants, known as onshikin, from the imperial household budget between the years 1914 to 1945. My analysis focuses on the amounts of the grants, their recipients, and the decision-making process behind disbursements, as well as the media response they prompted. There were three categories of imperial household grants: (A) those disbursed to the imperial family, the nobility, high-ranking bureaucrats, and employees of the Imperial Household Ministry, (B) grants disbursed to the general public, and (C) grants that defy easy categorization into either (A) or (B). I demonstrate that grants classifiable as (B) were conspicuous immediately after World War I, during the Great Depression, and in the period of total war from 1938 through to 1945. The imperial household used the media to promote an image of the monarchy as a benefactor and therefore secure its position in times of social unrest. I also show that, at the very same time, the imperial household was disbursing sizable grants in category (A) with the purpose of winning the loyalty of the social elite. In contrast to category (B) grants, these disbursements were not made public, and rarely reported on. The argument here is that the imperial household in modern Japan secured support from both the general public and the elites by controlling information. title: Distilling the Forest: Wood Alcohol and Industrial Chemistry in the Early Twentieth Century
abstract: In the early twentieth century, American chemists sought new ways to produce fuel and organic chemicals from the nation’s forests through improved wood distillation technologies. Remote hinterlands such as Michigan’s Upper Peninsula, which housed the world’s largest and longest-running wood distillery, became centers of technological innovation as new companies transformed the region’s abundant forests into complex chemical compounds that fueled global commodity chains. The story of wood alcohol, including methanol and cellulosic ethanol, produced at the Cliffs Dow Chemical Company in Marquette, Michigan, and in Germany reveals how a global network of extraction, technological exchange, and the politics of war catalyzed the organic chemical industry in the United States. This history illustrates the legacies that chemical innovations from the twentieth century have left on communities today.

title: Intelligence, espionage, and tribal collaboration: the Indian National Army and Japanese involvement in Northeast India during the Second World War
abstract: The enigmatic relationship between Japan and India underwent a significant transformation during the Second World War. The 1940s French Indochina crisis marked a turning point, prompting Japan to collaborate with Indian revolutionaries in Southeast Asia and with indigenous tribal groups across the Indo-Burma frontier. This alliance facilitated joint intelligence and espionage operations targeting British India, an aspect of wartime history that has received limited attention. This article examines how these covert networks advanced Japan’s vision of ‘Pan-Asianism’ while simultaneously bolstering the Indian independence movement, most notably during the 1944 Imphal-Kohima campaign. Drawing on archival materials, intelligence, interrogation reports, and topographical analyses, this study sheds light on this overlooked aspect of wartime history. It uncovers the complex interplay between regional alliances, intelligence collaboration, and ideological mobilization that influenced both Japan’s wartime strategy and the trajectory of the Indian national movement within the broader Asian context.

title: Living Among the Logwood: Maya Forests, Liminal Amphibians, and Quotidian Connectivities in the Laguna de Términos, 1667–1717
abstract: During the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries, the forests, wetlands, savannas, and mangroves of Laguna de Términos, the world’s largest tidal lagoon by volume, became a key site of interconnection in the Greater Western Caribbean Basin. Contrary to the region’s reputation as an isolated, empty swamp from which English loggers poached dyewood from Spanish territory, the coastal lowlands were connected by networks of nonhumans, Mayas, English, Africans, and Spaniards living among the dyewood stands. By decentering the primacy of dyewood and examining these other relationships, this article underscores the ways in which quotidian interactions substantially blurred imperial, cultural, and species divisions. Mundane activities, like eating and everyday exchanges, made the lagoon a destination, not a backwater, and became the mechanism by which multiple layers of Caribbean interactions coexisted and mixed.

title: Memories of the future: Olympic ceremonies, national narratives and the Anthropocene (2008–2024)
abstract: In the late 1970s, Reinhart Koselleck argued that expectations of the future are historically shaped by the relationship between experience and anticipation, a perspective later expanded by Fredric Jameson and others through analyses of literary and cinematic productions. While such studies illuminate cultural hopes, fears, and anxieties, they largely overlook one of the world’s most influential sites for imagining the future: Olympic Opening Ceremonies. Broadcast to billions of viewers, their hour-long artistic performances are collectively produced through collaborations involving governments, organising committees, artists, and cultural institutions, making them distinct from literary and cinematic works as nationally curated representations of the future. Through teleological narratives that connect a nation’s past, present, and future, Olympic ceremonies articulate national aspirations while positioning host countries within broader global imaginaries. Drawing on video recordings, official reports, media guides, and newspaper coverage, this article examines how the Summer Olympic Opening Ceremonies between 2008 and 2024 represented the future in response to the Anthropocene, particularly climate change and, later, the COVID-19 pandemic. It argues that, while Olympic futures remained embedded in national historical narratives, they increasingly reflected a shared horizon of expectation shaped by planetary crises, marking a shift away from earlier imaginaries centred on …

title: Facing the Tiger: Colonial Biopolitics and Animal Agency in The Tiger
abstract: Abstract This article examines The Tiger (Park, 2015) as a cinematic study of the conditions under which nonhuman animal life becomes politically visible, grievable, and agentive within colonial modernity. Situated within the symbolic economy of the tiger in Korean culture, intensified under Japanese rule, the article argues that Sangun, or the “Mountain Lord” in the film, is produced as “bare life” through a biopolitical apparatus of classification, surveillance, and annihilation. Drawing on Agamben (1998, 2003) and critical animal studies, the article shows how colonial governance produces the tiger’s “killability” through law, territory, and spectacle. The article moves to examine the film’s image economy, demonstrating how cinematic techniques such as close-ups and the return of the gaze to the animal’s face create an ethical address that resists allegorical incorporation. Finally, the article analyzes Sangun’s nonhuman agency, reconfiguring the sovereign asymmetry of the hunt and exposing the colonial machine that renders life disposable.

title: The Politics of Energy in Colonial Suriname
abstract: Abstract In colonial Suriname, a society shaped by slavery and indenture, the infrastructure and technologies of energy arrived as extensions of a colonial order that had long concentrated resources among elites. Drawing on colonial and company archives, this article shows how working-class Surinamese women and men engaged with gas and electricity, destroying street lamps one day while demanding connection the next. During the tumultuous 1930s, these communities protested against unequal access to power, exploitative labour practices at energy plants, and the racialized logics of privatization. As a monopoly in a small colonial society eager to expand its customer base, the European energy utility was compelled to respond to these demands. Yet even as energy use crossed from public into private space, working-class households continued to thwart colonial expectations that it would appease them, instead adapting these technologies to the survival of their own social worlds. Whether on the street or in the home, working-class engagement with energy revealed an ambivalence towards colonial modernity that challenged the terms of its imposition. This examination of how energy became a site of conflict shaped by a Caribbean plantation context thus extends energy history beyond its usual focus of the Global North.

title: Father Jiggs in Shanghai: The Rise and Fall of Comic Strips in Republican China in Transnational Context
abstract: Abstract This article traces the popularization of modern comic strips in Republican-era Shanghai via such strips serialized in the English-language newspaper The China Press. Consumed by both foreign and Chinese readers, these comics were some of The China Press’s most attractive features, especially George McManus’s strip Bringing Up Father, which appears to have been nearly universally known in Shanghai. From around 1920, the characters, form, and visual vocabulary of comics such as Bringing Up Father increasingly permeated Shanghai media and society, with significant overlap between English- and Chinese-language publications and audiences. The use of comics for advertising purposes played an especially large role in familiarizing Shanghai readers with comics, culminating in the appearance of the first major serialized Chinese-language comics in 1928. A central factor in this local establishment of comics as a transnational narrative technology of modernity appears to have been their contemporaneous embrace by periodicals published in Japan, which were widely available in Shanghai. Japanese military aggression during the 1930s conversely would preempt the continued development of Republican Chinese comics.

title: Flattening and Unflattening Space: Photography and the 1975 Okinawa International Ocean Exposition
abstract: Abstract Through an analysis of photographs produced in and around the 1975 Okinawa International Ocean Exposition, this essay develops the concepts of flattening and unflattening in material and visual registers. In line with the construction championed by Prime Minister Tanaka Kakuei, the Ocean Expo demonstrates that the Japanese state took post-reversion Okinawa as a space to be flattened into the mainland. Drawing on a phenomenological approach to space, the essay explores photographs published in Ocean Expo News, an official publication of the Ocean Expo. These promotional photographs visually flattened out the land around the expo site. In this way, they oriented Okinawa within cartographic space, ready for assimilation. The essay also examines a series of photographs taken on the Amami Islands that the mainland photographer Nakahira Takuma made in response to the Ocean Expo. Through consistently disorienting photographic space itself, they suggest a mode of unflattening. Photographs taken by Okinawan activist Ahagon Shōkō of land on Iejima also warp the cartographic space of the state and the US military, as if pushing through the second dimension into the third. Taken together, these three groups of photographs suggest that an unflattening of space might happen through the body.

title: Continuously Leaving the Closet: A Queer/Crip Approximation to Kondō Ginga’s Artworks
abstract: Abstract This essay examines the intermedial practice of Japanese artist Kondō Ginga, situating her work within the historical and theoretical contexts of postwar disability activism, queer/crip discourse, and feminist interventions in Japan. Through close readings of her works The Notifications (2021), Queer Street (2021), Separated (2022), Continuously Leaving the Closet (2022), and Prides in Streets (2024), the essay proposes that Kondō’ oeuvre renegotiates the intersections of digital and physical space, public and private visibility, and queer and disabled subjectivities. Kondō’s practice is analyzed along three dimensions: (a) the dissolution of the digital-physical divide; (b) small-scale, affective forms of reworlding and activism; and (c) sustained self-articulation across mediated and relational contexts. Historical case studies, from Ueno Park’ 1948 queer resistance to figures such as Yokota Hiroshi, Yonezu Tomoko, Asaka Yūho, and Hanada Minoru, contextualize her interventions, revealing continuities in gendered/queer and disabled visibility, exclusion, and resistance. The essay argues that Kondō transforms embodied limitation, chronic illness, and digital mediation into a politics of intimacy and care, redefining activism beyond public protest. Her work enacts “crip world-building,” demonstrating that survival, relationality, and aesthetic intervention constitute simultaneous, iterative forms of queer/disabled presence, challenging conventional notions of …

title: Scale: Temporal
abstract: The temporal scale of animal behaviour, the fact that animals adapt, change, and generate histories over time, remains one of the most systematically neglected dimensions of the disciplines of both history and ethology. This paper traces the intellectual and historical roots of that neglect from Aristotle, through dominant Christianity, to the adynamic frameworks of twentieth-century behaviourism and Lorenzian ethology. It argues that, while the spatial scale of behavioural differences within a species is now well recognized, time continues to be considered a neutral backdrop rather than a real factor in animals’ lives. Recent developments, however, including Japanese ethological work on macaques in the 1950s and Jane Goodall’s biographical and sociological analysis of chimpanzees in the 1960s, suggest that a properly temporalized animal history is now genuinely possible. The paper makes a methodological proposal: that historians and ethologists work in tandem, cross-referencing documentary sources with ethological knowledge rather than subordinating one to the other. This would open animal research at the scales of species, social groups, and individuals to questions of behavioural periodization, cultural transmission, and biographical singularity. Animals, in short, are no more outside time than they are outside space.

title: The Pig, Unspeaking
abstract: This article examines the representation of human language and its limits in the short story “The Pig of the Furandon Agricultural School” (c. 1921) by the early twentieth-century Japanese writer Miyazawa Kenji. The story features a domesticated pig, fluent in human language, who is slaughtered for his meat despite displaying a level of linguistic ability generally perceived as exclusively human. The pig’s literacy does not save his life; rather, it renders his experience of the human world more horrific, as he overhears what humans say about his edible body, peruses a death consent form he is subsequently coerced into signing, and comes to realize the transformation into meat that awaits him. In Miyazawa’s story, therefore, the nonhuman animal’s understanding of human language proves irrelevant to a pre-existing hierarchy of lives organized along species lines. As the pig becomes aware of his fate, the text ceases to textualize his speech and psyche, as if refusing to further territorialize the pig within human semantics, while continuing to describe how he appears, sounds, and behaves through onomatopoeia. This article foregrounds the ways in which Miyazawa’s depiction of the pig exposes the limits of human language and offers a glimpse of a world not entirely bound to an anthropocentric semiotic system.

title: Alicia Volk, In the Shadow of Empire: Art in Occupied Japan
abstract: This monograph is a critical survey of Japanese art during the understudied period of American occupation (1945–1952). The author outlines major developments in Japan’s metropolitan art world follo...

title: Counter-protesters against hate speech in Japan: negative framing by police, media, and activists
abstract: Abstract In 2013, counter-protests emerged in Japan in response to escalating far-right demonstrations featuring hate speech. Counter-protesters formed a movement described as “Liberal Antifa.” Many used Antifa symbols, yet the movement remained non-violent and distinct from the more militant Antifa in other Western countries. They verbally confronted far-right activists and used electronic noise, helping reduce far-right demonstrations. From the summer of 2025, their visibility once again increased through protests against the Sanseito. This paper examines how, despite these contributions, counter-protesters have been negatively framed across three layers: policing, news coverage, and activist discourse. Using forty-six qualitative interviews with forty protesters (2017–2023) and content analysis of activist publications and news reports, this study investigates the framing process and effects. It shows that these layers mutually reinforced negative portrayals, where policing with arrests on minor charges and media reliance on police press releases or sensationalism prioritised “law and order” over protest rights. Furthermore, activist discourse used historical analogies to delegitimise counter-protesters. This study elucidates the current dynamics of social control in Japan, including the blurring of boundaries between institutional media and online activist discourse, which leads to stigmatisation of counter-protesters.

title: An empirical study on the complex network characteristics of the Japanese language
abstract: Abstract This study selects eight registers of modern Japanese: interview, speech, official document, sci-tech text, political commentary, essay, poem, and novel, as corpora. Undirected and unweighted Japanese word co-occurrence networks are constructed using MeCab and Gephi. Based on complex network theory, this paper investigates the small-world and scale-free properties of Japanese linguistic networks. It applies quantitative tools: Erdős-Rényi random network benchmark, small-world index S, two-way analysis of variance, nonlinear fitting, piecewise regression, and Bootstrap resampling. Power-law tests follow the Clauset et al. method. Results indicate network size and register type exert significant main and interaction effects on small-world strength. The theoretically critical node number for small-world emergence is ninety-one, the empirical threshold eighty-nine, both falling within the 95 per cent confidence interval (81–146), confirming consistent theoretical and empirical findings. However, after removing high-frequency function words such as particles and auxiliary verbs, the network S-values are generally lower than 3, the threshold effect disappears, and the small-world property becomes unstable. The small-world property is neither an inherent attribute of the Japanese lexical system nor a direct outcome of the internal structure of word co-occurrence; instead, it heavily relies on the grammatical scaffolding constructed by high-frequency function words serving …

title: Teaching Authoritarian History
abstract: Authoritarianism 101: A Global History is a set of thirty primary source-driven teaching modules designed to offer teachers and students a broad perspective on the history of authoritarianism. The AHR commissioned historians working on authoritarian histories in Africa, Asia, Europe, Latin America, the Middle East, and North America to write teaching modules that explored a singular instance of an authoritarian past. Temporally, they range from the seventeenth to the early twenty-first centuries, with the bulk of modules concentrating on the long twentieth century. In this issue of the journal, we feature a selection of modules from the project that explore authoritarian histories in China, the United States, Egypt, Cube, India, Argentina, and Korea. All thirty of the modules that make up Authoritarianism 101: A Global History, along with additional teaching materials, are free to access on the project website. Among the supplementary materials highlighted on the pages that follow are a set of short videos and podcast interviews with some of the contributors to the project that explore how they came to create their modules, the larger issues around the history of authoritarianism they want to raise, and ideas for successfully teaching their modules in the classroom.

title: Inside the History Lab
abstract: The September 2026 History Lab focuses on the imaginative ways in which historians are using archives and other primary sources in their research and teaching to transform our understandings of the past. It opens with “Reading Nature’s Archives,” a forum that foregrounds new approaches to the research and writing of environmental history. Organized by David Biggs, the forum brings together a team of distinguished environmental historians who each offer short essays centered on a reading of a particular object or visual form of documentation. Their “archives” range from ivory figurines, whale bones, roof tiles, porcelain earthenware, and botanical prints to a colonial era cattle census, photographs of the sun, aerial imaging of former warscapes, and a twenty-sided golden cosmic box. Together, the contributors provide a set of novel critical methods for reading these sources attuned to how situated forms of knowledge about nature are often shaped by longer histories of borrowing, theft, erasure, and resilience. As Biggs argues in his introduction to the forum, the essays model what Achilles Mbembe calls “a planetary library or archive” that can remake historical apprehensions of the intertwined worlds of human history, nature, and technology.

title: Financing mission societies, capitalizing Protestantism: A transimperial history
abstract: Abstract This article examines the transimperial fundraising practices of two major continental European Protestant missionary societies—the Paris Evangelical Missionary Society (PEMS) and the Basel Mission (BM)—between the end of the Napoleonic Wars and the 1870s. It proposes a meso-level approach to global history that focuses neither on individual actors nor on abstract categories such as capitalism or religion, but instead on organizations. By analysing the PEMS and the BM, the article shows how missionary societies connected specific subregions of British India and Southern Africa with Protestant regions across the northern transatlantic world. Drawing on rarely studied financial reports, it demonstrates how these societies mobilized hundreds of thousands of donors through global financial networks spanning Europe, North America, and the colonies. In doing so, the article reframes Protestant missionary societies not merely as cultural actors but as economic institutions that helped normalize capitalist practices in both Europe and colonial settings. It thus contributes to transimperial and global history by suggesting a way to study Protestant continental Europe, the United States, and the British empire as mutually constitutive partners.

title: Coconut frontiers and ecological frictions in the Pacific World, c .1900–20: A multispecies history of capitalism
abstract: Abstract The copra industry that developed in the Pacific region from the mid-nineteenth century was a global, thriving enterprise. Imperial powers and trade companies jointly set up palm tree plantations that shaped the livelihoods of island societies and recruited Chinese contract labourers. Such monocultural territorialisations also radically transformed the environments and lives of non-humans (plants, insects, fungi), creating ecological conditions that challenged the same economic endeavours at work. ‘Economic entomology’, a novel branch of the scientific study of insects related to profit-oriented land management, emerged globally in the early twentieth century to protect plantations more efficiently from insect pests and other plant diseases. By focusing on the unprecedented outbreak of rhinoceros beetle ( Oryctes rhinoceros ) in the Samoan islands during German colonial rule and its aftermath in the Pacific world, this article examines the history of coconut capitalism in this region as a more-than-human history and explores the potential of reading the global archive against the grain while applying a multispecies ethnographic lens. In so doing, it reconsiders both the colonial anxieties exposed by the beetle outbreak and the kind of multispecies spaces that this insect opened up for Samoan resistance. title: Negotiating the Colonial Dilemma Through Science Fiction: Translating Jules Verne in Early Twentieth-Century Colonial Korea
abstract: Abstract This article examines the emergence of science fiction (SF) in early twentieth-century Korea by analyzing the first two Korean translations of Jules Verne—Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea (1907–8) and The Begum’s Fortune (1908). It argues that these relay translations, produced during the years between the Russo-Japanese War and formal Japanese annexation, reveal how Korean intellectuals navigated what the article terms the “colonial dilemma”: the challenge of rethinking national identity amid accelerated modernization and encroaching imperial domination. Rather than passively importing European SF, Korean translators actively reshaped the texts through genre relabeling, annotation, and selective adaptation, using them simultaneously as vehicles of scientific enlightenment and as tools for articulating Korea’s precarious place within global geopolitics. The article further contends that the early Korean use of the term “science fiction”—predating its standardization in the Anglophone world—calls for a reconsideration of global SF timelines and assumptions about the genre’s origins. By situating Korean SF within the broader East Asian circulation of Verne’s works and by highlighting the translators’ interventions into colonialist narratives, this study demonstrates that SF in Korea emerged not as an extension of European imperial imagination but through a complex interplay of colonial, anti-colonial, and nation-building impulses.

title: Archaeological Translation: How to Translate Diasporic Korean Literature
abstract: Abstract Min Jin Lee’s Pachinko chronicles four generations of Zainichi (Koreans in Japan) from the colonial era to the 1980s. Its translation process remains enigmatic; Lee imagined the narrative in Korean and Japanese before writing the novel in English. Consequently, the English original and its two Korean translated versions produce divergent meanings. This article investigates the translational issues in the two Korean versions, questioning the hierarchical order between the original Anglophone text and its translations. Building upon postcolonial translation scholarship, we first examine restored dialects in the Korean versions that are absent in the English text, analyzing their intersection with discourses of class, gender, and ethnicity. Second, we compare the opening sentences of the three versions, unearthing distinct insights into colonial and postcolonial histories embedded within each text. By unsettling conventional notions of originality, this comparative analysis introduces a new framework termed “archaeological translation.” Through this lens, we critique Lee’s mode of representation that flattens cultural and historical specificity, while demonstrating how translated versions evolve into distinctive texts with their own historical, political, and cultural perspectives in the transnational age.

title: Reading O Changhwan Translating Sergey Esenin in Seoul, 1946
abstract: Abstract This article explores the allegorical layers of meaning that emerge from one translator-poet partnership in the aftermath of the collapse of the Japanese empire in Korea. The iconoclastic modernist poet O Changhwan’s first published book in a newly liberated Korea was a translation of poems by the deceased Russian poet Sergey Esenin. O was translating at a moment when the Korean language was returning to public life after suppression under colonial rule and amid escalating violence on the partitioned peninsula. Reading O’s translations and lengthy afterword opens a window onto the scene of Seoul in 1946, one year before O was to cross over the thirty-eighth parallel into the northern zone. With the aim of rethinking the creative legacies of the early Cold War, this article explores the many meanings created in and through O’s translation.

title: Fraught friendships: East German experts, communist development, and environment in Mongolia during the Cold War
abstract: Abstract This article examines East German experts’ participation in development projects in Mongolia and their conceptions of environments during the Cold War. Starting in the 1950s, East Germany (German Democratic Republic, GDR) and Mongolia intensified economic ties that aimed to industrialise Mongolia and align with communist objectives. The endeavours were intended to provide development aid, though they also provided the GDR with access to natural resources it could not obtain domestically. Drawing on sources from numerous German archives, this article argues that East German development projects followed broader patterns of exploitation and consumption between Europe and the Global South after the Second World War. Communist trade relations dissolved with the end of the Cold War, but they set the stage for trade and environmental impacts that have continued to this day.

title: The Irrational Computer: Randomness and Unreason in the History of Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Abstract How did the computer, a machine built for logic and calculation, come to model the messy human mind? To answer that, ‘The Irrational Computer’ breaks with a familiar narrative of rationalization and quantification that stretches from the Enlightenment to the Cold War. Against this story of rational mastery, this project shows how influential British and American engineers came in the middle of the last century to see controlled chaos as essential to machine intelligence. They intentionally injected randomness into otherwise deterministic systems to achieve their desired result: ‘a slight error of reasoning’. Archival records, technical reports, internal memos, and popular coverage reveal the appeal and controversy of randomness in the history of AI. Rooted in theories of invention, modernist art, and wartime mathematics, notions of randomness allowed engineers to mechanize and materialize murky conceptions of creativity, intuition, and the unconscious. The evidence is abundant, but the argument is simple: today’s AI emerged from the conviction that replicating original thought required modelling not only logic but something deeply human, in other words, the irrational.

title: Reframing Cheongwadae (the Blue House) as a post-colonial place in South Korea: from Palace Garden of a Lost Kingdom to a seat of modern authority
abstract: Abstract Since the late 1980s, post-colonial discourse based on anti-Japanese imperialism has influenced the place-making of national facilities in South Korea. This study examines the spatial transformation and post-colonial discursive shift through the changing place identity of Cheongwadae (the Blue House), analysing the 1989 master plan for its reconstruction and the contentious debate over its reuse following its public opening in 2022. The research reveals distinctive aspects of South Korea’s post-colonial discourse, showing how the 1989 master plan created a symbolic national space by reproducing traditional architectural styles and introducing new urban axes that reconnected Seoul’s historical landmarks to Cheongwadae as a project of nation-building. The 2022 opening exposed conflicting ideas about Cheongwadae’s place and identity, both as a historical site of the lost kingdom and as a national symbol of modern authority. Specifically, the naming politics surrounding Cheongwadae revealed that preserving this political site in South Korea has become more significant than restoring the rear garden of Gyeongbokgung Palace, reflecting South Korea’s shifting post-colonial discourse. This suggests that the restoration of Joseon Dynasty heritage – once driven by anti-Japanese sentiment and symbolised by the “Correcting the Past” movement – is no longer a singularly dominant strategy for representing national identity.

title: The Virtual Reality Oracle: deeply mapping the oracle of Zeus at Dodona
abstract: ‘The Virtual Reality Oracle: Deeply Mapping the Oracle of Zeus at Dodona’ presents the development and creation of the Virtual Reality Oracle (VRO), a VR experience of visiting the ancient Greek oracle of Zeus, at Dodona, in NW Greece, on June 7th, 465 BCE. Challenging the metaphor of time travel as an accurate description of what the VRO offers its users, this essay investigates how we might better understand the nature and genre of such experiences. It draws on three different theoretical approaches: Michel Foucault’s concept of heterotopias, which was initially an approach to historical spaces, and Mikhail Bakhtin’s concept of chronotopes, a literary analytical device, before turning to the theory/process of ‘deep mapping’ as used, in particular, by Mike Pearson and Michael Shanks. It argues that this approach may offer a deeper under30standing of the nature of the experience of the VRO, and of the idea of time travel in this context – suggesting that users are themselves engaged in a process of creation of the past.

title: Eschatological Recognition and Spiritual Differentiation
abstract: Abstract This article examines how the Japanese Holiness leader Nakada Jūji interpreted the Māori religious movement led by Tahupōtiki Wiremu Ratana during his visit to New Zealand in the 1920s. Rather than approaching the Ratana movement as a distinct religious tradition, Nakada understood it within a universal Christian horizon shaped by his eschatological worldview. Drawing on his letters and writings, the article shows that he initially recognized the movement as a form of spiritual awakening but later reassessed it as theologically incomplete. This shift reflects a hierarchical mode of inclusion grounded in a developmental understanding of spiritual maturity within salvation history. The case demonstrates how transnational religious encounters could be framed not as exchanges between equal traditions but through classificatory frameworks that combined theological universalism with differentiated assumptions about human development.

title: Women Challenge Patriarchal Authoritarianism
abstract: ... On February 12, 1983, the Pakistani women’s rights organization Women’s Action Forum (WAF), in collaboration with the Punjab Women Lawyers Association, gathered hundreds of women for a nonviolent march on a main thoroughfare of the city of Lahore. They marched while carrying petitions against a newly proposed law, the Qanoon-e-Shahadat (Law of Evidence), and eventually staged an impromptu sit-in near the High Court. The proposed law defined women as secondary citizens, making a woman’s testimony in court worth only half that of a man. This prejudicial law would have wide-reaching consequences, particularly in the determination of cases of rape and assault against women. The protest was a pivotal event for anti-authoritarian movements in Pakistan as the first march to defy the total ban on public assemblies under the military dictatorship of General Zia-ul-Haq. The women’s march was met with a violent show of force from the state. The police charged the crowd with raised batons (lathi), beating people and arresting dozens of women. They fired teargas shells to break up the crowd, creating an environment of chaos and fear.

title: “TO SEUNAGAN SEEKING HAS SPREAD”: THE TRANSMISSION OF ESOTERIC TRADITION AND HISTORY AS PROPHECY
abstract: ABSTRACT In this essay, I explore accusations of heterodoxy, as well as rebuttals of these accusations, leveled at Sufi groups in late‐colonial and independent Aceh, the last region of what is today Indonesia to fall under Dutch colonial rule. What has been at stake in debates about the orthodoxy of such groups has not simply, or even primarily, been questions of proper belief or practice but concerns over historical and interpersonal relationships among participants in esoteric traditions. Following Nancy K. Florida's attentiveness to the ways in which “prophetic history” entails engagements with the past that entwine people across temporalities, I argue that accounts contesting the alleged heterodoxy of esoteric traditions in Aceh have been infused with an emphasis on seeking active and ongoing relationships across time and space, a mode that I identify as an intercessionary form of prophetic history. The proponents and detractors of any particular tradition make their claims not simply by referencing authoritative precedents but by cultivating relationships with those who populate the pasts that they invoke. This reframes orthodoxy as an ethical act of prophetic historiography.

title: Microhistory and Women’s Time Use
abstract: Abstract Gender historians have pioneered attention to ‘doing words’ to identify otherwise invisible women’s work. Searches in court records for verbs with female subjects have documented women’s widespread participation in economic activity, often directing and managing, while playing down their unpaid care for family members. This article turns to a microhistorical source, diaries written by Peter Walkden, a farmer and Nonconformist minister living in eighteenth-century Lancashire. Walkden’s account of his farming routine and interactions with family and community incidentally describes the activities of his wife, Catherine. Evidence of her ‘doings’ identifies Catherine’s repertoire of tasks but is extended here to identify work and labour relations by the ownership of equipment, production for use or sale, and the need for occasional stand-ins when Catherine was indisposed or unavailable. Additional circumstantial evidence and other historical and modern sources enable the estimation of the frequency and duration of tasks, so providing the first breakdown of an early modern woman’s working day. Findings confirm the extent of women’s work but reinstate unpaid care as vital to the functioning of Walkden’s household, and by inference to social reproduction generally. Significantly, when Walkden himself had to provide care or pay for an understudy, it was understood as work and its value recognized.

title: Insufficiently Dried Rice: The Conflict Between Socioecology and Technology Adoption in Colonial Taiwan
abstract: When Japan incorporated Taiwan into its imperial rice supply chain in the early twentieth century, it soon encountered trading difficulties caused by insufficient drying of Taiwanese rice, which it sought to overcome by promoting thermal drying technologies. However, these efforts saw limited success prior to the end of colonial rule. Drawing on archival research and employing perspectives from science and technology studies, this article situates farmers’ technology adoption within Taiwan’s socioecology of rice, which shaped local perceptions, values, and social relationships regarding rice drying and constituted specific economic rationalities, market cultures, and agricultural practices. The modern thermal dryers that were introduced, while aligning with Japanese commodification demands, were poorly articulated with the local socioecology and thereby failed to replace the sun-drying method. The experience of colonial Taiwan highlights the development of technology in relation to diverse organizing principles of socioecology, illuminating how the adoption of agricultural modernization technologies hinges on radical transformations in human–environment relationships within a society.

title: Draining Lhasa: The Long History of Kyisho’s Aquatic Enclosure and Urban Desiccation
abstract: This article traces 1,500 years of human engagement with the water cycle of Kyisho, the floodplain surrounding Lhasa, Tibet. As successive states made Lhasa their capital, Kyisho’s residents and rulers had religious, political and technological imperatives to divide the plain into wet and dry zones. Early cultivators practised irrigation but avoided the sacred sites of lha lu (deities and spirits). The rulers who introduced Buddhism in the seventh century drained marshlands to build the Jokhang and Ramoché temples. Later residents constructed embankments to protect them. As the Mongol, Manchu and British empires extended their influence into Tibet, Lhasa became a centre of pilgrimage and trade, prompting its enriched elites to expand Kyisho’s embankments and their riverside estates. Drainage accelerated after 1951, following Tibet’s incorporation into the PRC and the widespread use of industrial concrete. Intensive construction in the 1990s and 2000s caused environmental degradation. This was followed by the national ‘ecological civilisation’ policy, which sealed Kyisho’s remaining wet zones to conserve them.

title: Unity in Diversity? Nature Conservation in the Habsburg Empire
abstract: This article recovers the neglected history of nature conservation in the Habsburg Monarchy and situates it within a European context. Focusing on the Monarchy’s western half (Cisleithania), we trace how debates after 1900 reached Austria’s highest politics unusually early – beginning with a 1901 Reichsrat motion and an empire-wide 1903 survey – yet failed to yield implementation. We examine why this initiative stalled, how it affected the formation of a wide-ranging conservation movement and how these trajectories shaped post-1918 policies in Austria and Czechoslovakia. Along the way, we analyse evolving concepts ( Naturdenkmal, Naturschutz, Heimatschutz ), thematic priorities and the imagined communities invoked within and across imperial, national and linguistic lines. Our account draws on contemporary newspapers, association journals and scientific publications, as well as documents from archives in Vienna, Innsbruck, Koblenz, Berlin, and Prague. It positions the Habsburg case as a critical counterpoint to the nationalist frameworks in other European countries.

title: Reclaiming Fishermen’s Paradise: History of Waste Reefs in Southern Florida
abstract: This article examines the emergence and transformation of waste-based artificial reefs in southern Florida during the late 1960s and 1970s. It traces how early community-led efforts to restore declining fisheries, grounded in local ecological knowledge and practical experience, developed into large-scale projects that used discarded tyres and other waste materials. Drawing on newspaper accounts, scientific publications and corporate archival materials, the study shows how businesses such as Goodyear and the Deltona Corporation appropriated reef-building to address their own waste-management, reputational and regulatory concerns. As corporate actors increasingly shaped the practice, reef-building shifted from grassroots ecological restoration to a means of disposing of solid waste at sea, publicly framed as environmental improvement. The long-term consequences – including the instability of tyre reefs, widespread ecological damage and costly public clean-up operations – reveal how restoration rhetoric obscured material risks and redistributed responsibility to state agencies and volunteers. By analysing how practical, regulatory and promotional logics became intertwined, the article demonstrates how environmental interventions can be transformed when they begin to serve the interests of larger actors, and highlights the need to scrutinise the processes through which environmental practices acquire legitimacy.

title: Bloody Trade: Use of Slaughtered Animals’ Blood in Agriculture
abstract: In the nineteenth century, industrialised countries started using Peruvian guano as a fertiliser to meet the agricultural needs of their growing populations, but the material was almost depleted within a few decades due to excessive demand. The search for alternative fertilisers with a high nitrogen content led to manure production from organic urban waste, including animal blood. The agricultural use of blood as manure deserves closer study, since it is a vital substance that was obtained through the mass slaughter of animals. This article argues that blood manure represents a striking case of human domination and exploitation of other species. By examining the attempts at agricultural use of animal blood in industrialised countries and the Ottoman Empire, the article focuses on the dynamics involved in its commodification and aims to contribute to discussions on the emergence of the fertiliser industry, transformations in agricultural production and the changing relations between humans and animals.

title: From Moscow to Cologne and across the Atlantic: Newspaper science and the global origins of Soviet mass communication
abstract: Abstract This article situates early Soviet studies of the press, a specific academic field called gazetovedenie , within the global history of mass communication research. While scholarship often portrays Soviet media theory as entirely subordinate to agitational practice, this situation only became established by 1930, when well-known Soviet orthodoxies on the nature and role of propaganda fully solidified. In the 1920s, Soviet press scholars actively engaged with contemporary global debates about the press’s role in mass society, how propaganda functioned, and why it often failed. Far from working in isolation, they drew upon thinkers such as Karl Bücher, Grant Hyde, and Walter Lippmann, while developing distinctive approaches, including applying Formalist methods to media texts, that resonated internationally. Viewing this intellectual activity as part of a global exchange redefines the origins of propaganda studies, not as a Cold War divide, but as diverging, yet deeply entangled, responses to modernity, war, and mass politics.

title: Camera Time
abstract: Abstract In the early decades of the twentieth century, scores of men, women, and children around the world used the camera to enact their aspirational selves. While the power relationship inherent in some photographic encounters has been amply theorized, historians have been less concerned with a deeper understanding of ordinary personal portraiture, and especially its mimetic and ludic character. This essay focuses on such ordinary photographs commissioned or produced by middling urban Egyptians in order to make several methodological and historiographical interventions. First, I argue that these photographs ought to be understood as creative productions, rather than reflections or documentations of a self, and are best approached as dense social performances through which their subjects cultivated and realized some of the key desires unleashed by processes of urban modernity. Second, I employ these photographic acts to intervene in several recent debates, such as the place of enchantment in modern societies, the production of the Modern Girl around the world, and the articulations of local modernity in colonial situations. Paying attention to ordinary photographic practices brings new insights into these debates, as it also highlights the centrality of the camera to the emergence of modern forms of selfhood.

title: How Cold War Populism Can Promote Authoritarianism
abstract: Tonight as we celebrate the 141st birthday of one of the great men in American history, I would like to be able to talk about what a glorious day today is in the history of the world. As we celebrate the birth of this man, who with his whole heart and soul hated war, I would like to be able to speak of peace in our time, of war being outlawed, and of worldwide disarmament. These would be truly appropriate things to be able to mention as we celebrate the birthday of Abraham Lincoln. Five years after a world war has been won, men’s hearts should anticipate a long peace, and men’s minds should be free from the heavy weight that comes with war. But this is not such a period—for this is not a period of peace. This is a time of the Cold War. This is a time when all the world is split into two vast, increasingly hostile armed camps—a time of a great armaments race. Today we can almost physically hear the mutterings and rumblings of an invigorated god of war. You can see it, feel it, and hear it all the way from the hills of Indochina, from the shores of Formosa right over into the very heart of Europe itself. title: Archiving Asia
abstract: Abstract: Blue-and-white porcelain-inlaid earthenware, found exclusively in the 1600 San Diegoshipwreck and the Philippines, represents a distinctive material convergence within early modern global trade networks. However, the motivations behind the production of these objects and the perceived value attributed to them during that period remain unclear. Through integrated archaeological, visual evidence, and extant craftsmanship, this study investigates the cultural significance of the ware. While the production technique follows the barros Estremoztradition, the essay suggests that the ware’s creation was not merely driven by European nostalgia. Instead, drawing on the knowledge of búcaros’ sensory qualities among early modern European elites, it posits that the sensory experiences these objects offered provided Iberians with an alternative means to archive and engage with Asia, reflecting broader colonial ambitions and highlighting how the material properties of clay, minerals, and porcelain shaped early modern engagements with the natural world.

title: “Federal preservation”: The Strategy of Tōa Dōbunkai, a Quasi-Nongovernmental Organization in Japan during the Eight-Nation Alliance’s Invasion of China
abstract: Abstract The Eight-Nation Alliance War against China, which occurred during the Boxer Rebellion in the early twentieth century, represented both Japan’s earliest joint military operation with Western powers against China and the first involvement of a Japanese quasi-nongovernmental organization (QNGO) in an international issue. A prominent Japanese QNGO, Tōa Dōbunkai, intervened in the incident with the aim of ensuring “federal preservation.” This organization attempted to establish a so-called federal state that was independent of the Qing government yet subject to Japanese influence, primarily by persuading and assisting senior officials in southern China who exhibited a certain “independent” tendency, as well as anti-establishment forces during the incident. However, owing to the refusal of independence by senior officials in southern China and the defeat of the anti-establishment forces by the Qing army, this policy was eventually replaced by the more urgent Hokushin-ron policy, which focused on countering the Russian occupation of Northeast China. By reconstructing this historical process on the basis of primary sources, this study analyses the similarities and differences between the ideas and actions of Japanese QNGOs and the policy of the Japanese government towards China. On this basis, the research seeks to reveal the distinctive role of Japanese QNGOs in Japan’s early expansion into China.

title: Black-on-Black Makeup and the History of Blackface
abstract: Abstract This article contributes to transnational perspectives on blackface by examining evidence of Black individuals and communities employing darkening make-up or black masks on both sides of the Atlantic. It challenges the assumption that all such practices derive from, or are analogous to, black minstrelsy in the United States. Drawing on historical and ethnographic sources, the article situates these performances within local and transnational festive traditions, particularly those rooted in Afro-Iberian cultural practices, with many pre-dating US minstrelsy. In some instances, black-on-black blackface reproduces racist stereotypes or engages with the codes of White blackface minstrelsy; in others, it functions as a racially affirmative practice unrelated to US traditions. Cases from across the world reveal multiple meanings, ranging from resistance to stereotypes to the symbolic restoration of ancestral blackness and affirmation of racial pride. Taken together, the evidence makes plain the need to interpret black-on-black blackface within its specific historical and cultural contexts. Furthermore, it calls attention to the transnational circulation of Afro-Iberian traditions of racial impersonation, largely overlooked in scholarship, alongside the diffusion of US minstrelsy. By foregrounding these alternative genealogies, the article contributes to a more nuanced and globally informed understanding of blackface and ethnic impersonation in the Atlantic world.

title: On the Uses of Whale Bodies for History
abstract: Abstract Whales are participants in history. While they do not create written archives, whales capture in their bodies the specific details of their individual lives as well as the societies in which they have lived. Fortunately, the long history of whaling has left behind an underappreciated, globe-spanning archive of whale history in the form of biological artifacts, like bones, teeth, baleen, and ear wax plugs. Through a survey of some of the latest research into paleobiology, this paper highlights how historians can use the information bound up in these natural archives to recount the journeys, diets, companions, and emotional states of whale societies across years, decades, and centuries. In doing so, historians can expand our spectrum of analysis to include non-human animals in their own right; to see how certain creatures shaped human history, but to also consider whale histories of the world.

title: Citizenship and autonomy: Bilateral labour migration governance and its discontents in Malawi, Mexico, and Spain, 1919–75
abstract: Abstract During the 1930s, the International Labour Organization sought to establish standards for bilateral labour migration agreements on separate but parallel colonial and nation-state tracks. I interrogate the ramifications of these discussions across the subsequent half-century, integrating global structural scales of analysis with migrants’ perspectives on the ground. First, I trace the concept of the ‘temporary migrant worker’ in the bilateral migration agreements signed in the 1930s to the 1960s between Spain and France; Nyasaland (later renewed by independent Malawi) and South Africa; and Mexico and United States. I then show how common post-war ideas and pressures led Mexico, Spain, and Nyasaland/Malawi to invest local authorities with substantial control over emigration and deprioritize migrants’ comfort and safety. Migrant-generated sources, notably letters, petitions, and oral histories, point to a resultant convergence of experience unanticipated by international policy discourses: migrants coming to perceive their own states as a primary barrier to progress, dignity, and autonomy.

title: Dancing ambassadors: The Indian republic’s global cultural project
abstract: Abstract Beginning in the 1950s, emerging from the British empire’s shadow, the Indian government helped dancers become globe-trotting, state-sponsored cultural ambassadors, projecting a vision of the young nation’s art as ancient, sophisticated, and spiritual. Asserting a ‘national culture’ (understood by the formerly colonized as essential to decolonization) involved its reconstitution, despite claims to civilizational continuity. This article reveals how dance became the natural candidate for global cultural projection, the ways in which the state allied with artists in this endeavour, and the conflicts this engendered between them. It offers insights into the state’s anxieties about the nation’s image globally, debates within civil society and between politicians about Indian culture, and the logic underlying how Indian dance was presented differently across the world. The global projection of culture and its reception abroad was part of the contested process of defining it at home. National culture took shape as it travelled the world.

title: PERIODIZING GEOLOGICALLY OUTWITH (AND WITHOUT?) THE ANTHROPOCENE: PASTS, AGENCIES, AND THE TERRESTRIAL
abstract: ABSTRACT As a periodization that is generally understood to refer to an era of Terrestrial relationships that developed with modernization and nuclearization, the Anthropocene cannot be applied simply to premodern histories and texts. However, it has introduced historians to geological periodization as a mode of describing periods of changed Terrestrial relationships in time. This article suggests that, in thinking about how historicizing texts conceptualized environments, geological (“‐ocene”) periodization provides a useful model and grammar by which to observe and describe how authors understood their environmental pasts, the agencies involved in reshaping Terrestrial regimes, and the role of environments in periodization. This article uses two genres of historicizing texts from Western Britain in the twelfth century to develop an approach to reading geological periods out of such texts. It suggests that doing so not only reveals important information about how these authors thought about environments in time but also provides a model by which the “geological turn” in the environmental humanities and premodern history can be put into mutually productive conversation without being inappropriately constrained by a term that was developed for modern phenomena. Outwith the Anthropocene, reading texts for what they say about environmental pasts, times, and agencies enables environmental thought to be analyzed in multiple dimensions.

title: ASSEMBLING PASTS, PROJECTING FUTURES: READING TINTIN WULIA'S A THOUSAND AND ONE MARTIAN NIGHTS WITH NANCY FLORIDA'S WRITING THE PAST, INSCRIBING THE FUTURE
abstract: ABSTRACT In Writing the Past, Inscribing the Future: History as Prophecy in Colonial Java , Nancy K. Florida identified a form of Javanese historical writing in which telling the past is a political act, one oriented to envisioning possible futures. This essay examines an experimental video by the artist Tintin Wulia that resonates with this prophetic form of history. Wulia's video, A Thousand and One Martian Nights , blends documentary and science fiction to tell the stories of political prisoners sent to the island of Buru as if they were exiles cast away to Mars in 2065. Footage from the United States’ space program in 1965 contributes to the futuristic tone while setting the decimation of the Indonesian leftist movement within the context of US imperialism. This layered video unsettles the conventions of historical evidence and linear narrative, eschewing conventional documentary forms that the New Order regime appropriated for state propaganda. Wulia's collaged historical text challenges the evidentiary claims that underpin conventional historiography and reimagines the past to open paths toward more just futures. By staging an unlikely dialogue between Wulia's video and Florida's reading of the Babad Jaka Tingkir , this essay aims to extend the efficacy of Florida's text. It argues that, however profoundly engaged it is with a specific literary tradition and historical context, Florida's text offers us generative ways to think broadly about the politics and potentials …

title: NOT QUITE A PROPHET FACING BACKWARD: ON HISTORY AS EXTENSION OF PROPHECY
abstract: ABSTRACT This essay develops the concept of history‐as‐extension‐of‐prophecy , a mode of historiographical reasoning that unsettles the dominant modern opposition between tradition as temporal continuity and revolution as temporal rupture. Through a close reading of Aḥmad b. ʿAbdallāh al‐Saqqāf's (1882–1950) Tārikh Sulṭanat Bāntan al‐Islamiyya , a mid‐twentieth‐century Arabic history of the Islamic Sultanate of Banten (West Java), I show how prophetic temporality operates as a form of historical extension, linking past, present, and future through an inherited script whose fulfillment remains open, deferred, and actionable. Drawing on Nancy K. Florida's account of Javanese “history‐as‐prophecy,” I demonstrate that al‐Saqqāf mobilized prophecy not as eschatological closure or antiquarian devotion but as a historiographic method that renders time morally legible and political generative. Through the concept of miṣdāq (extension), al‐Saqqāf aligned dispersed episodes of anticolonial resistance and Islamic revival with a prophetic ḥadīth about a continuously “victorious group,” thus reframing Indonesian history as an unfolding exegesis of Muḥammadan truth. I propose that history‐as‐extension‐of‐prophecy illuminates a distinctive temporal politics, one that carries inherited promises forward while activating unrealized possibilities in the present. It neither binds political life to a fixed past nor surrenders it to revolutionary novelty. Instead, it mediates continuity and …

title: JAKA TINGKIR: ANCESTOR, KING, SAINT—FRAMING A JAVANESE HERO IN A POPULAR SONG
abstract: ABSTRACT As Nancy K. Florida stated in Writing the Past, Inscribing the Future: History as Prophecy in Colonial Java , in the more dominant historical traditions, Jaka Tingkir is recalled as the founder of the Central Javanese kingdom of Pajang, an ascetic, an exile, and a brave warrior. Well‐known from chronicles such as babad texts and other storytelling genres, the figure of Jaka Tingkir has inspired artists to reinterpret his appearance and role in their own creations. In this essay, I discuss an early twenty‐first‐century song that, in part due to its reference to Jaka Tingkir, became wildly popular and extremely controversial. Focusing on dialogic encounters (a key concept in Florida's work), I explore how, in their responses to this song, religious leaders not only reiterated historical narratives and cultural practices but also put these into new contexts, creating new pasts while envisioning future aspirations.

title: What is UNRWA for? The contested purposes of refugee relief in Gaza, 1948–1950
abstract: Abstract In the midst of the crisis of displacement caused by the 1948 war for Palestine, the newly minted United Nations contracted with the (Quaker) American Friends Service Committee to provide aid to Palestinian refugees in Gaza. Over the next eighteen months, as AFSC workers participated in the institutionalization of new and modern forms of internationalist refugee assistance, many of them came to think that the real goal of this regime was not protection or succour but order, containment, and prolongation—a conclusion that informed the AFSC’s decision, in 1950, to withdraw its provision of aid and turn over its operations to the new United Nations Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA). This article explores this brief and apparently minor historical interregnum in Palestine’s refugee regime with an eye to the enormously consequential questions it raises: who built these modern refugee regimes, what did they actually do, and to what ends?

title: INTRODUCTION: REFLECTIONS ON HISTORY AS PROPHECY, CONTINUING THE CONVERSATION
abstract: ABSTRACT In this essay, I provide brief introductions to the notion of “prophetic” historiography that I developed in Writing the Past, Inscribing the Future: History as Prophecy in Colonial Java (1995) and to the five essays of this forum that were written in dialogue with it. I argue that “history as prophecy” forms a practice of writing in which the “prophetic historian” seizes hold of a moment of past potency to self‐consciously reinscribe it in the historian's present so that it may become a context for action in the futures of its readers. In my book, that argument is developed by means of a deeply textured reading of a unique nineteenth‐century narrative history of Java's fifteenth‐century transition to Islam, a nearly seven‐thousand‐line poetic history that was written by a royal exile. Each of the five essays engages my notion of “history as prophecy” in conversation, extending it into other realms of historical expression. The subjects of these five essays include contemporary performance cultures in Indonesia, an Arabic‐language Islamic history of the Indonesian past, genealogical practices of Acehnese Sufis, and Indonesian literary history.

title: TEMPORALITIES OF FREEDOM: DID NANCY FLORIDA'S BABAD JAKA TINGKIR “PROPHESY” MARCO KARTODIKROMO'S STUDENT HIDJO ?
abstract: ABSTRACT In her discussion of two episodes in the Babad Jaka Tingkir , a little‐known and incomplete nineteenth‐century Javanese narrative poem that is part genealogical history and part fictional romance, Nancy Florida asserted that these episodes, which are the two most “novelistic” episodes in the Jaka Tingkir “history,” hint at a new kind of historical writing. In this essay, I begin by interrogating what Florida meant when she called the Babad Jaka Tingkir “a historical prophecy” and then consider whether Student Hidjo (A Student Named Hijo), a 1918 novel written in Malay prose by a Javanese journalist and novelist, Marco Kartodikromo (1890–1932), can be interpreted as a fictional representation of what Florida termed “a new historiographic project” rather than as merely an interesting literary echo of a Javanese “history” written fifty years earlier in colonial Java.

title: REENCHANTMENT, INEFFABILITY, AND “THE DIALECTIC OF NOMINALISM”
abstract: ABSTRACT Martin Jay's newest book, Magical Nominalism: The Historical Event, Aesthetic Reenchantment, and the Photograph , aims to reveal the presence of a third current of thought in modern thinking. This current, which he calls “magical nominalism,” does not fit the traditional dichotomies (voluntarism–determinism, subjectivism–realism, and so on) around which the field's prevailing narratives are organized. As he shows, magical nominalism participates in the process of destroying the Scholastic idea of a perfectly ordered cosmos (an idea that was initiated by nominalism in the fourteenth century) but introduces into the nominalist matrix of thought a reference to an ontological dimension of reality that was initially absent from it. However, as he insists, magical nominalism does not constitute a homogeneous current. This form of thinking resists definition in unequivocal terms. Studying it therefore requires an approach that is capable of articulating a plurality of views.

title: Solar Photography
abstract: Abstract The mid-nineteenth century adoption of the new technology of photography transformed astronomical and meteorological practices. Today, there are upwards of ten million astronomical photographic negatives in observatory collections—a fraction of which are undergoing digitization to contribute to growing online databases of the astronomical archive, such as Germany’s Archives of Photographic Plates for Astronomical Use (APPLAUSE) and Digital Access to a Sky Century at Harvard (DASCH). As scientists revisit these images for time-domain astronomy, historians too are attuned to their significance to understanding the material conditions of their production. Focusing on a specific sunspot group, this essay situates these surviving plates in the visual and material cultures of astronomy and meteorology in the British colonies in the early twentieth century. It argues that such photographic plates, used in conjunction with more conventional documentary sources, can shed light on contemporary cultures of weather watching and forecasting.

title: Emerald Sea and Red Roofs
abstract: Abstract Red tile roofs are the icon of the Chinese coastal city, Qingdao, favored by German colonizers, Japanese invaders, and, most importantly, millions of Chinese who have resided in and built the city. This essay argues that, rather than treating them merely as cultural symbols, the red roofs, along with the cityscape they adorn, are a material artifact that blends both natural and cultural elements. They form a type of nature’s archive, recording the entangled environmental and cultural past of the city. We can learn to read and interpret these archives by analyzing our shared biological roots, the clay, the fuels, the tile-making process, the material sediments stored in the roofs, and the disposal process at the end of the tiles’ lifespan. By approaching the red roofs this way, they are no longer simply a German colonial heritage imposed on this Chinese city. On the contrary, we come to recognize a more complex history of the city, shaped by both external natural materials and our own inner desires and practical needs.

title: Cattle Censuses
abstract: Abstract Colonial historians have analyzed how human population censuses were instrumental for state-making and ethnic categorization, and how they can be used for demographical reconstruction. By contrast, they have thus far ignored the significance and analytical potential of livestock censuses. This essay teases out their potential for historical analysis by focusing on cattle censuses in French colonial Madagascar (1896–1960). It argues that colonial authorities went to great lengths to count cattle, deemed a key economic resource of the island, and showcase their numerical evolution in statistics, graphs, and maps. Due to context- and species-specific limitations of the data, historians cannot easily use these censuses to reconstruct cattle demography. Yet, they offer a fruitful lens to analyze cattle policies and knowledge regimes under colonial rule. Censuses were both an instrument of knowledge, used to monitor the evolution of the herds and reconceive policies, and an instrument of extraction, on which the annual cattle head tax was based. In both cases, cattle censuses were also sites of contestation. Tax extraction warranted strategies of dissimulation from the part of cattle owners, making knowledge even more unstable and causing epistemological anxieties within the colonial administration.

title: Literary Expression at the Ends of Unicode
abstract: Abstract This article examines how Unicode reshapes the humanities by asking what happens when a supposedly universal encoding system meets the demands of the Japanese writing system. Focusing on EnJoe Toh's 2018 collection A Whirlpool of Glyphs, it shows how his fiction probes the tension between standardization and expression that underlies script reform from the Qin dynasty to contemporary Unicode debates. EnJoe's stories stage conflicts between inclusion and exclusion—what counts as an encodable character, which graphic forms are discarded, and how these decisions constrain or enable writers working with Sinographs, kana, and their visual and expressive possibilities. By dramatizing everything from Qin-era script reforms to rebellious furigana and proliferating variant characters, EnJoe makes visible the technical infrastructures that underwrite the process of writing. In doing so, the article argues, he exploits the Japanese writing system's capacity for orthographical variation at the limits of possibility. Unicode functions simultaneously as a tool of global standardization and a platform that “standardizes the nonstandard,” with significant consequences for how the humanities preserve, classify, and imagine written forms, and EnJoe's work offers a key case for understanding how script technologies condition literary creativity across languages and periods.

title: Reading Conflict Landscapes
abstract: Abstract Intervisual analysis, using Geographic Information Systems to compare historic satellite imagery with ground-sourced information and maps, offers new methods for analyzing changes in conflict landscapes over time. By pairing visual data with local studies, oral histories, and texts, one may better appreciate visual biases in imagery and reveal hidden landscapes and histories. Intervisual approaches demonstrate how modern conflict sites like Phu Bai airfield often overlap with more ancient conflict zones and their spatial footprints can linger long after hostilities have ended.

title: Ivory as Archive
abstract: Abstract This paper explores how historians might read ivory as an archive of environmental history. Using six figurines from Ming and Qing China held at the Eskenazi Museum of Art as a case study, it situates them within three histories: one of modern collecting; one of early modern production; and one that foregrounds elephants themselves. Ivory itself is a kind of archive. Biochemical signatures within it record key aspects of elephant lives, including their diet, lineage, and geographic origin. In the case of the Eskenazi figurines, these signatures showed that the collection derived from elephants from six different regions, two different continents, and two different eras. Connecting the elephants’ histories to human ones requires a participatory and omnivorous approach to environmental history: building partnerships with museums and citizen-historians, interpreting historical texts, and collaborating with scientists. The approach affords the opportunity to relate human histories to the history of life on Earth on the one hand, and to grow the community invested in environmental history on the other.

title: Displaced women, law and competing patriarchies in late Ottoman Serbia
abstract: Abstract Focusing on women who were displaced, unclaimed, or left without protection in the shifting legal order of early nineteenth-century Ottoman Serbia— runaway wives, enslaved and manumitted women, fugitives, and kidnapped girls —this article argues that the burdens of transition into the modern state were experienced most acutely by women who fell through the cracks of overlapping spatial and legal regimes of control. Despite their varied circumstances, women shared a structural problem: they had no pathway to legal personhood, no rights to return to or leave their homes, and no protection unless recognized within a patriarchal household. Their legal belonging remained tethered to household authority even as new centralizing political and legal orders took shape. In this unstable transitional period, patriarchy was distributed and enforced across competing scales and legal structures, including households, villages, Ottoman imperial institutions, and emerging Serbian state structures. Drawing on Serbian court and administrative records from the 1820s–30s, this article traces how various local and imperial officials negotiated these tensions, suggesting that transitional legal systems inscribed gendered asymmetries into modern practices of repatriation, citizenship, trafficking, and statelessness.
