title: Institutionalization and Market Integration in the Archaic Greek Economy: Modelling Overseas Trade from the Distribution Pattern of Samian Transport Amphoras
abstract: Abstract This article advances the view that there was widespread institutionalization in the early Greek economy from the end of the eighth century bce. Challenging the widespread assumption that Mediterranean market integration crystallized much later and only by the end of the ‘archaic period’, agent-based modelling is used here alongside the archaeological distribution of Samian transport amphoras to demonstrate the coordination that must have existed between trade partners in shipping olive oil from one end of the Mediterranean to the other. ‘Brownian flow’ models of randomized drift fail to properly reproduce the amphora pattern, while a model based on a network of trade hubs stretching from the Black Sea to the shores of modern-day Spain provides a much more robust solution. These results shed light on the navigation of various environmental niches, on the lived experience of the sailors distributing products such as Samian olive oil, and most importantly suggest that the early Greek economy was more organized— and earlier, too —than we have previously suspected.

title: Between commerce and sanctity: Ottoman policies and international boundaries in the early modern Red Sea
abstract: Abstract This article examines the transformation of the Ottoman empire’s maritime boundary policies in the Red Sea during the early modern period. It focuses on the dual character of the Red Sea, as both a religious frontier safeguarding the Holy Cities and a strategic maritime corridor within global trade networks. Drawing on Ottoman and British archival sources, the study analyses the period from 1517 to 1798 in three distinct phases: a closed sea era shaped by the Portuguese threat (1517–1608); a phase of negotiation with friendly European actors (1608–36); and a period of controlled openness (1636–1798), in which limited access was granted to merchants recognised as müsteʾmin (protected foreigners). The article argues that Ottoman maritime sovereignty in the region was not exercised through absolute control, but through a flexible and negotiable mode of boundary management. This perspective offers a contribution to early modern debates on imperial border-making and sovereignty by revealing how empires balanced ideological commitments with economic pragmatism.

title: Archive of the Seven Spheres
abstract: Abstract: During the last decades of the eighteenth century, the Kingdom of Mysore in southern India became immersed in reading the stars to ascertain its fate in times of war against the British East India Company. Seeking to know the order of the universe and its influence on the Earth, advisors and astrologers in the court of Tipu Sultan, the nawab of Mysore, compiled a library of Persian and Arabic manuscripts on the planetary sciences of astronomy (ʿilm al-nujum) and astrology (ʿilm ahkam al-nujum), including original texts synthesizing Persianate and Sanskritic knowledge of the celestial sphere. In the pages of this planetary archive, the cosmos—comprised of the seven planets of Islamic astrology—was mirrored by the climes of the Earth. Through knowledge of the stars and their movements and the use of talismanic objects to mediate planetary influences, the kingdom could divine and shape its future. This essay introduces this archive of the astral sciences, and explores elements of its visual and material culture, to trace views of the Earth and its place in the cosmos from the eighteenth-century Deccan.

title: Seriously Chaotic
abstract: Abstract This paper examines ran nō 乱能, an unconventional kind of nō performance that features parody, role inversion, and improvisation in an otherwise solemn and formalized art form. While nō is grounded in ritual and religious themes, ran nō introduces humor through unorthodox casting and playful gags, often during festive occasions. Focusing on historical records and a case study of the 2009 Shukuga Ran Nō in Kyoto, where even sacred themes were treated with playful irreverence, this study traces the origins, evolution, and functions of ran nō . This paper argues that ran nō fosters cohesion among performers, amateurs, and audiences by allowing for a controlled moment of transgression that ultimately reaffirms the values and structure of the nō tradition.

title: Food Security, Nitrates Capitalism, and the Haber–Bosch Revolution
abstract: Abstract This article reinterprets the early history of the Haber–Bosch process of ammonia synthesis through the transnational development of synthetic nitrogen production at Ludwigshafen am Rhein and Billingham-on-Tees, County Durham. It argues that the nitrates revolution in the early twentieth century was not simply a technological breakthrough but a contested project linking industrial strategy, state power, and food security. Tracing the British government’s wartime construction and subsequent privatization of the Billingham plant, it shows how economic orthodoxy constrained efforts to sustain state-led industrial co-ordination, even as private firms pursued cartelized forms of governance. It situates the British and German chemical industries within a shared political economy, and reframes fertilizer production as central to the emergence of modern food politics and the international political economy, anticipating later debates over sovereignty, inequality, and environmental limits. Recovering these histories reveals food security as a foundational problem of industrial modernity, with nitrates capitalism shaped by decisions about the governance of national resources, scientific expertise, and global markets.

title: The birth of Golden Week: rival adaptations of School of Freedom and the postwar constitution of Japan
abstract: The introduction of new liberties in Japan’s post-war constitution sparked nationwide debate during the final years of the Allied Occupation. Shishi Bunroku’s satirical novel School of Freedom (1950) captured the public’s fascination – and puzzlement – over this influential yet elusive notion. Serialised in Japan’s leading newspaper, the Asahi Shinbun, the story follows a married couple navigating the social realities of early post-war life. The salaryman husband abruptly abandons both his job and his marriage in pursuit of freedom, prompting his wife to reconsider her own life prospects. Following the novel’s success, two film studios swiftly acquired the rights, and their competing adaptations were released simultaneously in May 1951, coinciding with a newly established string of national holidays. This timing boosted audience turnout, and the unexpected surge in box-office earnings led a film executive to coin the term ‘Golden Week’, which soon became synonymous with the holiday period itself. School of Freedom thus left an imprint not only on Japanese cinema but also on the cultural imagination and leisure practices of the emerging consumerist nation. This article explores the production and reception of the rival films, situating them within the late Occupation-era popular discourse surrounding the new rights – and accompanying obligations – stipulated by Japan’s 1947 constitution.

title: Working borders: Mad Studies, psychiatric museums, and decolonization
abstract: This essay considers recent, contemporary ’mad studies,’ in their activist, academic and museological dimensions, especially in the 2000s. It attends to mad histories in relation to Global North/Global South borders and other decolonizing aspects, and the emergence since the 1980s of mad/asylum museums in European and African manifestations. The notion of ’working borders’ is engaged in relation to disciplinary academic borders but also as working in scholarly or public elements and strands. It especially contextualizes such working of borders in activist historical work, thus beyond psychiatric historiography and since the 1960s.

title: Care as resistance and care as hope: ecocritical affect in Tawada Yōko’s The Emissary and Fernanda Trías’s Pink Slime
abstract: This paper explores how representations of nonhegemonic politics of care intersect with environmental degradation to reimagine human-nature relationships. Through transpacific comparative analysis of Tawada Yōko’s Kentōshi (The Emissary) and Fernanda Trías’s Mugre rosa (Pink Slime), I argue for comparative literature between Japan and Latin America as a decolonial methodology for Japanese Studies. My goal is twofold. First, I examine to what extent we can approach alternative modes of care as a way to understand the ongoing call to transform our relationships with the environment caused by the climate emergency. Second, I will argue how understanding this production in ways that defy the boundaries of area and discipline strives to put into practice an approach to Japanese studies that is organically decolonial. By integrating methodologies from transpacific comparative literature, ecocriticism, and ecofeminism, this paper contributes to ongoing efforts to decolonise Japanese Studies through expanded geographic and methodological frameworks.

title: Reassessing we : toward heterochronic histories of Japan
abstract: This paper analyzes the general exhibitions at the National Ainu Museum (NAM) and the Okinawa Prefectural Museum and Art Museum (Okimyū) to propose a new heterochronic approach to Japanese histories that deimperializes the present Yamato-centric narrative. Beginning in 1868, the fledgling Empire of Japan rushed to establish itself as a modern nation by, on the one hand, colonizing its neighboring regions beginning with Hokkaido and the residing Ainu population to the north and the southernmost islands occupied by Ryūkyū, and on the other, promoting its cultural sophistication through the newly compiled ‘Japanese art history’ that focused solely on the cultural production of the Yamato ‘Japanese’. Today, the imperial chronology at the core of Japanese art history and any other historical discourse of Japan continues to orchestrate a sense of unbroken progress and restricts ‘Japanese-ness’ in Japanese Studies to ethnic Yamato. Opened over ten years apart, NAM and Okimyū use different strategies to subvert the imperial monochrony of the mainstream Japanese history in their general exhibitions that transmit the heritage and identity of the communities they represent. By analyzing how the two institutions assert alternate conceptualizations of time through their gallery organization, this study argues for decentering and de-normalizing the present singular and linear imperial chronology as the first step to envisioning a deimperialized (and decolonized) Japanese Studies.

title: Embracing women: affective power and transformative empathy in Kirino Natsuo’s Daku onna and Murata Sayaka’s ‘Kakusei suru itami’
abstract: Kirino Natsuo’s novel Daku onna (Women who Embrace, 2015) follows its protagonist, Naoko, as she struggles to find her place within the student movement and women’s liberation movement (ūman ribu) during the early 1970s in Japan. This article also considers Murata Sayaka’s commentary on the novel, ‘Kakusei suru itami’ (‘Awakening Pain’, 2018), in which Murata claims to relate to and share Naoko’s pain. This paper argues that the pain of this historical moment—mediated through fiction—resonates affectively across generations, eliciting readers’ empathy and sharpening their sense of historical injustice towards women. Daku onna encourages readers to embrace Naoko’s subjectivity and plight alongside their own, while creating empathic linkages, or ‘coalitions’, between characters in the novel, and between readers and writers too. This article identifies narrative and contextual strategies that augment the novel’s affective power among Kirino’s readers. First, I analyse the novel’s paratextual, metatextual, and historical dimensions—including its title, cover, promotional discourse, narrative’s context—emphasising the significance of the events in 1972. I then draw on feminist theorisations of empathy as transformative to explore how textual features in Kirino’s novel and Murata’s essay invite readers to engage affectively with Naoko’s pains as a means of processing generational trauma. title: Dead Bodies of the Okinawan Forest: Decolonial Subversion and Dangerous Nature in Medoruma Shun’s The Rainbow Bird
abstract: Post-war Okinawa has endured a complete reordering of its urban and natural spaces. The American administration expropriated lands from local communities for military bases, used Okinawa forests as storage facilities and training camps, and limited the local population’s access to significant places for remembrance and collective memories. This spatial reorganisation still stands today, even after Okinawa’s repatriation to Japan in 1972, foregrounding the importance of complex issues of land ownership and natural environment reclamation among Okinawan communities and external authorities. In his novel Niji no tori (The Rainbow Bird, 2006), Okinawan-born writer Medoruma Shun re-negotiates the position of the autochthonous environment and its non-human inhabitants within the Okinawan colonial establishment, decentring the human experience by proposing the forest as a complex actor whose agency impacts the colonial establishment. Through his writing, the Yanbaru forest emerges not only as a violently subversive site of decolonial contestation but also as an active character who works to resist the American colonizers and reclaim its independence from the Okinawan human community. title: Jeffrey S. Hardy. Finding God in the Gulag: A History of Christianity in the Soviet Penal System
abstract: In Finding God in the Gulag, Jeffrey S. Hardy tells the story of religious believers in the Soviet prison camp system. Although the Gulag—the system of forced labor camps in the Soviet Union—has been extensively researched, the story of religious faith in the Gulag is far less well known. Scholars have explored how faith and a sense of higher meaning and purpose helped people survive the dehumanizing environment of Nazi concentration camps. Although the history of Soviet atheism has received significant recent attention, the history of Soviet mass repression of religious believers has not. The Soviet regime did not simply disestablish the Russian Orthodox Church and institute atheist propaganda; it expended enormous effort to eradicate religion. Yet religion did not disappear: According to the suppressed 1937 census, over half of the Soviet population believed in God twenty years after the revolution, and the Soviets continued to battle against religious belief until the end. This book contributes to an important facet of that story.

title: Ted Binnema. The Vancouver Island Treaties and the Evolving Principles of Indigenous Title
abstract: The principal goal of Ted Binnema’s The Vancouver Island Treaties and the Evolving Principles of Indigenous Title is simple: present a “disciplinarily historical perspective” on a series of fifteen land purchase agreements drawn up between 1850 and 1854 that are today known as the Vancouver Island Treaties (6). As the only such agreements between Indigenous communities and colonial authorities in British Columbia before the colony joined Canada in 1871, these “treaties” have occupied an outsized place in the complicated landscape of Canadian jurisprudence. Binnema argues, however, that the legal importance of these purchases has tainted modern examinations with “juridical preoccupations” and “other presentist concerns,” leading him to conclude that “the scholarly literature on the Vancouver Island treaties is badly flawed” (5). The thirteen chapters of this book present Binnema’s ambitious efforts to right this state of affairs. Chapters 1 to 7 delve into the deep history of these purchases, examining the land policies of the Hudson’s Bay Company (HBC) going back to its first trading expeditions in 1668 (chapters 1 and 2), the evolution of human societies on Vancouver Island since time immemorial (chapter 3), and the interactions between newcomers and Indigenous communities from the arrival of Spanish explorers in 1774 to the first purchase agreement in 1850 (chapters 4 and 5). title: Radical accounting as method: interconnections across time, space, and bodies in Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater’s archives
abstract: This essay contributes to digital history by proposing ‘radical accounting’ as a method for gathering data from archives to support analysis of bodily practices at a scale that encompasses the transnational, intergenerational, and collective. Taking as our case study the Black-centered, multi-racial concert dance company Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater established in 1958, we manually curated data from over 30,000 print materials held by the Ailey Foundation, the Library of Congress, the New York Public Library for the Performing Arts, and the Black Archives of Mid-America, among others, to document all the artists who contributed to the company, all the dances that they made and performed, and all the places around the world where those performers and performances were seen. Through close analysis of datasets and experimental data visualizations, this essay demonstrates how radical accounting surfaces historical interconnections across performing arts ecosystems and artistic practices. While data ethics often emphasize incompleteness, radical accounting offers an alternative model for rigorous practices of care, drawing attention to the contributions of performers, contexts, and repertories relegated to the periphery of dominant historical narratives, and showing how embodied knowledge comes into being between and beyond all of these datapoints.

title: THE PHILOLOGY OF RACE IN LATE QING CHINA
abstract: ABSTRACT This article rethinks the problem of race from the late nineteenth century onward by examining how the concept of race configured an impasse in the relationship between history and nature in late Qing China. By analyzing the debate about race and history within late Qing philological discourse, it offers new readings of early foundational texts from China's long revolutionary twentieth century that address questions surrounding race, nation, and state. It takes late Qing intellectuals such as Zhang Taiyan, Liu Shipei, and Liang Qichao not as thinkers who were influenced by race but as thinkers of race—that is, individuals who scrutinized the coherence of a logic of race and its political possibilities. The fateful encounter between late Qing philology, the Kantian antinomy of race, and European comparative philology exposed the limits of a racial logic of reference by which the human was ordered on a global scale. This article locates within the reading and writing practices of late Qing philologists the demands on historical thought posed by a logic of race as well as its limits and contradictions. Thus, this article takes as its focus neither systems of racialization nor histories or genealogies of the concept of race. title: Surekha Davies. Humans: A Monstrous History
abstract: Surekha Davies declares that “[m]onsters are category problems that have to be defanged” (67) in her dazzling new book Humans: A Monstrous History. This politically engaged work shows how and why humans have “monstrified” other people across many different settings, deploying examples from histories of colonialism, gender, religion, science, and the environment in a deliberately wide-ranging work of accessible scholarship. Some of the most compelling and detailed examples come from the author’s background in the global history of the early modern period, but Davies adeptly juggles case studies ranging from the classical world to science fiction. She does so in order to ask the reader to assess the ethical implications of stereotyping others as “monstrous,” and to simultaneously argue for a positive, inclusive way of thinking about monstrosity through the lens of difference. These two strands are held in productive tension throughout the book. abstract: Scholars of French or Indian history (or indeed of European imperial or Indian Ocean history more broadly) might be puzzled by the book’s subtitle. They have not forgotten the history of French India. But Glorious Failure is not written for them. title: On the Place of “Meaning” in Traditional Festivals
abstract: Abstract In the literature about traditional festivals, the question of what the festival rites mean , or what they may have meant “originally,” is often at the forefront. Yet, in a fieldwork situation, festival actors tend to give seemingly random answers to such questions or make it clear that they are not relevant to them. On the other hand, festivals require constant investments of time and money, as well as access to public space, for which an explicit narrative of meaning is often necessary. What, then, is the place of meanings in festivals? This article uses the theoretical perspective of Humphrey and Laidlaw (1994) to analyze attributed meanings in the hanamatsuri festivals of Oku Mikawa, Japan. Tracing the history of narratives regarding the meaning of these festivals, I propose that while historical crises have at times called for radically new meanings, the development of festival performances has followed its own dynamic.

title: Confusion of Places
abstract: Abstract This article explores the concept of “escape ecologies”—landscapes whose physical and institutional illegibility allows people to evade coercion—by linking the present-day Białowieża Forest to eighteenth-century Eastern Europe. Based on field observations made during the state of emergency on the Polish-Belarusian border in 2021, this essay shows that modernized environments, including abandoned drainage ditches, collapsed spruce monocultures, and dense undergrowth caused by forestry practices, grazing bans, and climate stress might serve as effective corridors and shelters for migrants, despite the presence of drones, patrols, and fences. Juxtaposing these observations with early modern maps and administrative records reveals analogous mechanisms in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. In this context, unregulated rivers, wetlands, riparian forests, and river islands allowed deserters, fugitives, dissenters (e.g., Old Believers), and commoners to move about, hide, negotiate, and resist. Such a perspective challenges power-centric historiography, which overinterprets textual archives produced by rulers while undervaluing environmental archives and vernacular practices. Thinking through escape ecologies makes it possible to see why the poorly governed marshes and forests of Eastern Europe attracted fugitives, dissenters, and migrants alike—and why, despite the radically different technological conditions, they continue to do so.

title: Sarah E. Bond. Strike: Labor, Unions, and Resistance in the Roman Empire .
abstract: There is a long tradition of caution among Roman historians. Anachronism, modern terms, values, and frameworks can all easily overwhelm our fragmentary source base, creating false, overly modern interpretations. Our hesitancy has generated steady, but admittedly very slow, progress, especially on lesser-documented segments of the Roman population. We have struggled to effectively characterize, let alone categorize, some of these groups, as we seek to avoid importing baggage from other periods and fields of study. As Sarah Bond powerfully argues in Strike: Labor, Unions, and Resistance in the Roman Empire, we needn’t tie ourselves into knots to work on these portions of the populace. Anachronism, properly acknowledged and employed strategically, can be another tool in our kit, and it can be deployed to “return a voice of collective action to a conversation about labor in the ancient world” (5). Strike explores the power that existed within and was sometimes utilized by associations of workers in the Roman Republic and Empire. Bond begins in the near-mythological past of the city and guides the reader to the early Middle Ages in a comprehensive look at seven periods, each with distinct expressions of resistance from and attempts to control working people. The result is an accessible history of the Roman world that centers the experience of working people.

title: The Python God and the Empty Chair
abstract: Abstract This article explores how African royal power over the slave trade shaped transatlantic and cross-cultural interactions around sovereignty in the early eighteenth century. Employing an interdisciplinary approach, it analyzes the rich visual and material culture archive produced by the coronation ceremony of King Hufon of Hueda. This event offers a window into how Africans and Europeans negotiated, displayed, and subsequently reinterpreted cross-cultural relationships as part of competing political projects. By tracing the evolution of the story of Hufon’s coronation in Europe over many decades, the article shows how authors, artists, and publishers altered the memory and thus the archival imprint of Hufon’s power, obscuring the political subservience European merchants experienced in the kingdom. This formation of European imperial ideology occurred in parallel with a distinct but connected political process in West Africa, as the Dahomey kingdom overran and incorporated Hueda territory in response to the kingdom’s position within the Atlantic slave trade. The article argues that Hufon’s statecraft reverberated across African-European, inter-European, and inter-African relationships, demonstrating that the deep reconstruction of actual African-European relations in West Africa is necessary for understanding both Hufon’s coronation ceremony and how African power projected through Atlantic commerce shaped European and African imperialism.

title: Karin Wulf. Lineage: Genealogy and the Power of Connection in Early America
abstract: For far too long, the history of the family has been relegated to a secondary field of interest or even an area for genealogists rather than professional historians. In Karin Wulf’s adept hands, however, family history is essential for unpacking key historical questions about power, race, law, and gender. Lineage: ­­Genealogy and the Power of Connection in Early America offers a multi-layered, sweeping study of the way ­­eighteenth-century Americans deployed family histories as tools of governance and hierarchy. This richly illustrated, meticulously researched and argued book weaves together the latest innovations in cultural history to read a wide range of “texts.” Wulf’s voluminous source base ranges from a silver plate engraved with a family story to illustrated bibles to mere scraps of paper in archives across the eastern United States and England. Her mastery of the scholarship of “vast early America” (a term Wulf herself coined) allows her to contextualize her evidence in historiographies of family, law, religion, material culture, sexuality, and slavery. While this is primarily an Anglo-American story, Wulf situates the work in conversation with scholarship on the broader Atlantic world in this era.

title: Forever in Fiction
abstract: Abstract Against a backdrop of ongoing harm, this essay interrogates the limits of closure—in grief, nuclear decommissioning, and academic scholarship. I draw from an unexpected moment in my research on the Three Mile Island nuclear power plant’s sixty-year closure in which I discovered part of my personal history at the public library that caused me to reexamine how closure and containment operate in both the oral histories that people told me, and the academic training that calls for me to construct a tidy narrative from them. I compare this narrative form of closure in oral histories with the plant’s more subtle impact on everyday life, as well as my own endeavor to frame these fragments in ways that do not sacrifice their incoherence for a logical retelling of them. This essay challenges closure as a useful concept or method not only for nuclear decommissioning and grief but also for scholarship, and proposes the politics of resisting closure, particularly in the climate of late industrialism and capitalism.

title: An Absent Mother between Two States
abstract: Abstract Motherhood—one of the most important and yet mundane social institutions—is central to understanding the rise and decline of Third World internationalism. This article focuses on Francisca Casparina Fanggidaej (1925–2013), a left-wing Indonesian activist in the Afro-Asian solidarity movements that developed out of the Bandung Conference. She is also a mother of seven who endured decades of forced separation from her family. Based on a close reading of Fanggidaej’s diaries, personal letters, and oral history interviews with her family and friends, I discuss the politics of maternal absence in Indonesia and China—two of the leading countries in the Afro-Asian movements. I explore how these two countries shaped the public and self-perceptions of nonresidential mothers through their welfare provisions and reproductive policies. title: Shulamit Volkov. Germany through Jewish Eyes: A History from the Eighteenth Century to the Present
abstract: Since the beginning of “modernity,” Jews have repeatedly been an object of inquiry by non-Jews who evaluated and disparaged their subjects’ religion and lives. The sheer volume of ink spilled on discussing Jewish emancipation and Jewish rights during the long nineteenth century (and beyond) demonstrates how central Jewish lives and religion were to self-definitions of Germanness; however, the writing of German history has struggled mightily to incorporate Jewish lives in anything but a peripheral manner—right up to the present. Often, Jewish lives—if they are presented at all—revolve around suffering, discrimination, and the Holocaust. Furthermore, the view from the historians of German history rarely reflects the views of German Jews and the times, places, and spaces in which they lived. The field of German-Jewish history has thus flourished where German history has lagged behind, and such scholarship has provided a lens through which we can view how Jews lived in the German states and in the context of the events of their time. Yet these historiographical traditions are in an asymmetrical relationship—the latter relies explicitly on the former, but the former can pick and choose when, where, and how to incorporate the latter.

abstract: In How the New World Became Old, Caroline Winterer provides “a new history of the United States” by exploring the geological and paleontological studies that led to the realization of deep time, the multimillion-year-old history of life on Earth. “For many [present-day] citizens of the United States,” she writes, “the antiquity of the land is a core feature of their national identity.” Although a debatable point, this does not diminish her well-written and thought-provoking account of “how and why this view of ancient America came to be” over the course of the nineteenth century (1). Whereas many histories of American geology and paleontology have focused on specific controversies, such as the rivalry between paleontologists and fossil hunters Edward Drinker Cope and Othniel Charles Marsh, Winterer offers a sweeping narrative that defies easy characterization. title: Jack Neubauer. The Adoption Plan: China and the Remaking of Global Humanitarianism .
abstract: At first glance, Jack Neubauer’s The Adoption Plan: China and the Remaking of Global Humanitarianism appears poised to trace the transnational history of child adoption from China. But readers expecting an account of Chinese children adopted into families abroad will soon find themselves on a different track. Instead, Neubauer examines the early days of a now widespread fundraising strategy: international child sponsorship, through which individuals send money to support children in welfare institutions, focusing on creating relationships between donors and child recipients via the exchange of personal letters, gifts, and photographs. This program in China, which Neubauer refers to as “The Adoption Plan,” forms the book’s central subject. Neubauer follows the early twentieth-century histories of organizations employing this tactic in China—such as the National Association for Refugee Children, the China’s Children’s Fund, Foster Parents Plan for War Children (PLAN)–China Branch, and the American-Oriental Friendship Association—drawing on Chinese- and English-language archives and monographs, as well as eclectic English sources. title: Robert W. Galler Jr. Taking Charge, Making Change: Native People and the Transition of Education from Stephan Mission to Crow Creek Tribal School
abstract: Education histories about Indigenous students in the United States increasingly contend with the agency of families, students, and community members, even as they also document the schools’ violent policies and tactics. Robert W. Galler, Jr.’s Taking Charge, Making Change: Native People and the Transition of Education from Stephan Mission to Crow Creek Tribal School joins the growing collection of such histories by examining how the relationships between Catholic leadership and Dakota families influenced the local landscape at Stephan Mission boarding school from the early nineteenth century through the mid-twentieth century. As a local history situated within federal policy and international Catholic developments, Taking Charge seeks “to understand the connection between Native people and American education in a particular place” (19). Accordingly, it accounts for the holistic nature of establishing and running a school: the buildings, staff, curriculum and textbooks, funding, programming, and parental engagement. Galler has meticulously examined missionary sources, including letters between priests across a number of Catholic archives and priests’ own diaries. While reading for Native agency, this emphasis on Catholic sources also results in a deep engagement with the records of the priests themselves and a significant focus on their vantage points, positioning the book as a useful contribution to missionary school histories. title: TWO ACCOUNTS OF HISTORICAL KNOWLEDGE: HISTORIOGRAPHIC REASONING AND NARRATIVE ACCORDING TO AVIEZER TUCKER AND CHIEL VAN DEN AKKER1
abstract: ABSTRACT This review essay examines a recurring distinction in the philosophy of history between the phase of establishing historical facts or knowledge claims and the phase of interpreting them. Focusing on two recent books by Aviezer Tucker and Chiel van den Akker, it analyzes how each author conceptualizes historical knowledge by emphasizing one of these phases. Tucker locates the core of historical practice in evidential reasoning and the production of knowledge claims about past events, which he regards as the basis for consensus among historians. In contrast, van den Akker concentrates on the construction and understanding of narrative theses and argues that historical narratives are not direct descriptions of evidence but unique interpretations. This review essay argues that, although the distinction between research and interpretation can be somewhat useful, an attempt to synthesize Tucker's and van den Akker's accounts into a single and more comprehensive theory of historical knowledge would be problematic. Since each framework highlights one phase and leaves the other underdeveloped, a meaningful theory of historical work must be developed internally within one conceptual framework rather than assembled from incompatible accounts with distinct priorities.

title: Representations of precolonial androgyny and the figure of Tipu Sultan in Gidwani and Karnad
abstract: This article re-examines Tipu Sultan beyond colonial and nationalist representations that hyper-masculinize him as either predatory or benevolent. I use the term hyper-masculinization to describe a representational stratagem in which Indian rulers are depicted in lopsided extremes: either as excessively violent and aggressive or conversely as overly compassionate and weak. Such single-dimensional representations sideline the wider cultural meanings of masculinity associated with the traditional Indian conception of androgyny. This study fills this gap by arguing that Tipu’s personality is far more profound and many sided and can be better apprehended through the hitherto overlooked conception of androgyny, understood in Ashis Nandy’s work as a marker of masculinity in pre-colonial India. Here androgyny is not a form of gender ambiguity but a culturally bounded ideal of balance that sacralizes political agency, controlled violence, and creativity. Drawing on Ashis Nandy’s conceptualization of Indian masculinity as well as Hindu and Islamic metaphysical worldviews, I argue that Indian fictional writings such as Girish Karnad’s The Dreams of Tipu Sultan and Bhawan S. Gidwani’s The Sword of Tipu Sultan can be read as presenting Tipu as an androgynous sovereign. In doing so, these texts stand in sharp contrast to the colonial demonization and nationalist romanticization of Tipu as a hypermasculine individual. While neither Karnad nor Gidwani may have explicitly set out to recover …

title: Getting by but not getting ahead: Muslim families, community networks, and school lunch accommodations in Kumamoto City, Japan
abstract: As Japan’s Muslim population grows, religious accommodation in public schooling is increasingly pressing, yet existing research has focused on individual families and schools while overlooking Muslim community networks. This study examines why Muslim families in Kumamoto City are ‘getting by’ in securing school lunch accommodations but not ‘getting ahead’: why, despite an organised community centred around the Kumamoto Islamic Centre (KIC), parents continue negotiating individually rather than collectively. Drawing on interviews with Muslim parents and Japanese educators, the study employs a social capital framework distinguishing bonding, bridging, and linking capital. Families rely on co-ethnic bonding networks. Bridging capital within KIC has not been mobilised around halal because diversity of interpretation prevents a collective position from forming; without it, linking capital connecting the community to schools and authorities cannot develop. Three accommodation types are documented: an informal parent-led arrangement, a formalised shared-responsibility system (the ABCD system), and an institution-led full provision model. The ABCD system has the greatest potential for broader application. The study argues that the absence of a unified community position is a structural feature of how halal is practised in a diverse community, and that systemic improvement requires municipal frameworks that support school-level accommodation without presupposing collective consensus.

title: Bad fakes and the concept of success
abstract: This article explores the concept of a successful, or convincing, forgery. What makes a forgery successful and why? Drawing from a range of high-profile and lesser-known cases of forgery from the eighteenth to twenty-first centuries, this article examines the dominant notions of success in forgery and challenges the assumptions that uphold them. It demonstrates that although the conditions that enable the creation of a successful forgery are multifaceted and vary considerably, what exactly constitutes a successful forgery is inextricably linked with its capacity to deceive. However, by decentring the importance of deception in the makings of a successful forgery, this article makes space for thinking about the bad, childish fakes that occupy the lower ends of the antiquities market in particular as successful and in what capacity. It concludes by arguing that bad fakes, much like bad art or bad movies, can simultaneously embody multiple and at times radically divergent notions of success unrelated to their ability (or inability) to deceive.

title: The present state of Japanese research on the Chinese Communist Party: report on the joint review workshop “Great Dissection of the CCP”
abstract: Abstract The present article focuses on five recent Japanese-language research monographs on the history of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and the People’s Republic of China (PRC), authored respectively by Eda Kenji, Mishina Hidenori, Zhou Jun, Takahashi Nobuo, and Suzuki Takashi. The books cover a wide span, reaching from the history of the early years of the CCP through the Communist-Nationalist civil war era, the early years after the founding of the People’s Republic, the implementation of the Great Leap Forward policy, the Cultural Revolution, and until the contemporary Xi Jinping regime. Based on a joint review workshop held at the Institute for Research in the Humanities at Kyoto University in 2025, the article discusses the contributions of the five books and the perspectives of their respective reviewers.

title: A French revolutionary political club and its global contexts: The Society of Lorient, 1790–94
abstract: Abstract How can a political society established in one port city in Revolutionary France be a ‘global’ actor? This article examines the revolutionary Society of Lorient, an Atlantic port founded to be the seat of the French East India Company, as a case study of the viability of the ‘micro-spatial’ approach to global history outlined by Christian De Vito. It considers how the Lorient Society positioned itself as an intermediary between global concerns and the French national authorities, as well as the Society’s evolving perspective on global imperial rivalries in their relationship to revolution, the ‘rights of man’, trade, war, race, and slavery. In doing so, it shows how a seemingly local actor could help construct the global in the context of the ‘Age of Revolution(s)’ of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries.

title: The Tokyo Shichū Ongakukai: commercial bands and the informal spread of Western music in Meiji Japan
abstract: The adoption and spread of Western music in Meiji-era Japan (1868–1912) is often explained through formal, state-led initiatives such as military bands, educational reforms, and the establishment of institutions including the Tokyo Academy of Music. While these state initiatives created the infrastructure for musical change, they do not fully explain how Western music eventually came to be heard and enjoyed by the broader public. This article examines the role of commercially organised wind and brass ensembles in the informal diffusion of Western music during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. It centres on the Tokyo Shichū Ongakukai (Tokyo City Band), a privately organised band founded in 1887 that transformed military musical practices into entrepreneurial entertainment, giving performances at hotels, parks, and other urban venues in and around Yokohama. Drawing on a micro-historical reading of a 1942 interview with co-founder Ikeda Tatsugorō, the article reconstructs the everyday experiences of musicians navigating the emerging commercial and cosmopolitan worlds of Meiji Japan. Situating the band alongside related phenomena such as department store youth bands and mobile street ensembles known as jinta, the study argues that Western music spread not only through state institutions but also through commercial spectacle and consumer culture.

title: Thresholds of meaning: metaphor, conceptual change and historical imagination
abstract: This essay analyzes the structuring role of metaphors in contemporary historiography by engaging in dialogue with three key works: Key Metaphors for History by Javier Fernández Sebastián, Intellectual History and the Problem of Conceptual Change by Elías José Palti and History and Identity by Stefan Berger. Across three sections, it reconstructs the convergences among these proposals concerning the epistemic function of metaphors, understood not as stylistic embellishments but as figurative matrices that mediate between experience, language and historical interpretation. First, it examines how metaphors shape forms of historical reasoning and grammars of temporality. Second, it analyzes their role as catalysts of conceptual change, particularly in contexts of semantic crisis or epistemic dislocation. Finally, it explores the potential of a historical metaphorology to foster interdisciplinary dialogue among history, philosophy, political theory, visual studies and material culture. What is thus advocated is a critical renewal of historical theory – one capable of training historians who are aware of the tropological substratum of their practice and equipped with tools to intervene in public debates on memory, identity and the uses of the past. Metaphors, in this framework, not only serve to weave historical narratives, but they also make them possible.

title: Charting the shattered sea: Maritime geopolitics and transnational oceanography in East Asia, 1984–2007
abstract: Abstract This article examines the challenges of border-crossing science at geopolitical hot spots through the case study of the East Sea (also known as the Sea of Japan). The East Sea is a marginal sea on the north-west Pacific Ocean surrounded by four historically conflicted nations—South Korea, North Korea, Russia, and Japan. Despite vast scientific interest, severe military conflicts have restricted transnational cooperation in this region throughout the late twentieth century. Utilizing personal archives, cruise reports, and interviews with participating scientists, this article examines how an international team of East Asian oceanographers developed material, political, and rhetorical tactics to circumvent and even appropriate complex border problems at the end of the Cold War. The case study suggests that the global history of oceanography should pay further attention to the practical challenges of accessing geopolitically conflicted basins as well as creative strategies that scientists devise to bridge over those troubled waters.

title: Faith, Famine, and Resilience: The 1817 Subsistence Crisis during the Megadrought in Catalonia
abstract: The article analyses the social consequences of the subsistence crisis and water scarcity in 1817, one of the most severe years of the megadrought (1812–1824) that affected northeastern Spain. Drawing on municipal records from Barcelona, Tarragona and Girona, ecclesiastical documentation and commercial correspondence from a grain trading company, it examines how hydrological stress disrupted food supply, intensified conflicts over water access and shaped relations between rural communities and urban authorities. Harvest failure contributed to rising grain prices and increased migration in a post-war context marked by institutional fragility. In response, authorities and local institutions promoted charitable initiatives, public works and regulatory measures to secure water and grain supplies. Evidence from Urgell, an agricultural region of Catalonia, illustrates the scale of agricultural losses and peasant displacement. The study conceptualises drought as a socially embedded crisis shaped by prolonged environmental stress, governance constraints and unequal resource access.

title: Engineering Redemption: Francoist Colonisation Villages and the Making of Spain’s Fascist Landscape
abstract: This article situates Francoist colonisation villages within broader debates about nature and nation in twentieth-century fascist regimes. It argues that the Franco regime’s ambitious hydraulic program – dams and irrigation networks – must be understood both as a material reconfiguration of territory and as an authoritarian strategy for reorganising rural populations. Through the coordination of hydraulic engineering, agricultural planning and settlement construction, the Instituto Nacional de Colonización y Desarrollo Rural (National Institute of Colonisation) consolidated a new irrigated agrarian order while reinforcing existing landholding structures and producing technically trained, politically loyal subjects. Alongside these material interventions, newsreels played a crucial role in shaping the meanings attached to this transformed national nature, framing the domestication of water and territory as a providential project of national regeneration and representing colonisation villages as idealised rural communities. By analysing their cinematic representation, this article highlights the importance of visual construction in naturalising authoritarian modernisation while obscuring social conflict and ecological disruption. Colonisation villages thus emerge as key nodes in the fusion of hydraulic modernisation, political control and national mythmaking.

title: Narrating modern crisis and acceleration: re-reading Carl Schorske’s Fin de Siècle Vienna
abstract: In the late nineteenth century, the economic, social and cultural accelerations of western modernity triggered intensifying reactions, including racism, nationalism and communitarian politics, that sought refuge in tradition from the threat of change. Conversely, cultural movements emerged that embraced the dynamics of innovation. Carl Schorske’s Fin de Siècle Vienna: Politics and Culture, immersed in the complexity of these contesting responses enacted in a critical cultural and intellectual milieu of the period. Schorske sought resolution of fin de siècle crisis and acceleration through catharsis, presenting at least the possibility of a restoration of cultural unity; yet his narrative more convincingly described forces of disintegration generated by the drive for progress. Drawing on the work of Reinhart Koselleck and the debate on modern crisis and acceleration stimulated by it, Schorske’s seminal work is explored to develop a reconsideration of the intellectual and cultural energies generating progress and crisis at the fin de siècle and resonating into the twentieth century.

title: Unruly Singing and Shouting: Listening to Labourers’ Work Songs in Modern Shanghai
abstract: Abstract As early as the third century bce, references to labourers’ work songs appeared in the Chinese court-sponsored compendium Lushi Chunqiu, and, for the 2,000 years that followed, labourers throughout China continued to sing these songs. Despite variations in their tones, rhythms, and lyrics, their chanting performed some essential functions: synchronizing movements, communicating information, and boosting morale. During the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, however, the sound of such songs became controversial among newly arrived Anglophone settlers as well as Chinese intellectuals in Shanghai, evoking emotions ranging from frustration, contempt, and desperation to compassion, admiration, and even inspiration. This article historicizes the contested interpretations of Chinese workers’ singing and shouting, exploring how different listeners’ anxieties and agendas shaped what they heard. At the same time, it juxtaposes these reactions with the labourers’ own justifications for the sounds they made, and their responses to the baffling modern cityscape they had to navigate. While reconstructing the histories of marginalized groups has long been hindered by the perception of archival silence, attending to sonic traces often dismissed as ‘mere noise’ can help to recover the vital sounds of those otherwise rendered voiceless by the historical record.

title: Making history enjoyable: rules and resonance in the Romance of the Three Kingdoms video game series
abstract: This article examines how the Romance of the Three Kingdoms (RTK) video game series transforms history into a source of gameplay enjoyment. Moving beyond debates over historical accuracy and authenticity, it asks how history functions for video games rather than how video games serve history. The article analyzes RTK through two interconnected dimensions: the rule-based reconfiguration of historical materials and resonance between the game and players, understood as a twofold mechanism for generating enjoyment. The article argues that RTK reorganizes historiographical records, literary narratives, and modern media representations into a calculable game system structured through quantified character attributes, turn-based temporality, restricted historical agency, and conquest-oriented goals. Through these rule structures, historical complexity is translated into a framework that enables prediction, planning, and strategic decision-making. The gameplay experience is further recontextualized through resonance, as players relate emergent in-game narratives to their prior knowledge of the Three Kingdoms. By foregrounding the interplay between systemic abstraction, which constructs a generalized rule-based framework, and resonance, which reconfigures gameplay through individualized meaning-making, this article argues that historical video games do not simply represent the past but generate historically grounded enjoyment through the interaction among rules, players, and …

title: Staying vigilant during times of crisis: What shapes COVID-19 pandemic sensitivities?
abstract: During the COVID-19 pandemic, Japan recorded comparatively favourable public-health outcomes while relying largely on voluntary citizen behaviour. Existing scholarship traces this pattern to communitarian norms and discipline, the prevalence of exclusionary and coercive social practices, and bottom-up enforcement of public-health recommendations driven by perceived undersecuritization. We approach the puzzle through the concept of vigilance, meaning the configurations of attention that operate alongside formal surveillance and function simultaneously as social control and community care, enabling responses to complex crises beyond the reach of state mandate. Drawing on twenty-two in-depth interviews, three years of (auto-)ethnographic fieldwork in Tokyo, and complementary analysis of policy and media texts (2020–2023), we trace how pandemic sensitivities were shaped by the everyday texture of urban life. Four interacting factors emerge as drivers of sensitisation and desensitisation: practical knowledge about risk, the rhythm of disruptions to daily routines, the diversification of pandemic narratives, and the materiality of risk in the environment. Each factor can intensify attention to threat or absorb it into the mundane. As an unusually rich empirical case, COVID-19 reveals how vigilance regimes are produced and dissolved through urban daily life. These insights can sharpen the governance of latent, protracted, and complex public emergencies.

title: The plague of Egypt crossing the Red Sea: The arrival and focalisation of plague in the southern Red Sea region in the 1430s
abstract: Abstract Drawing on textual, archaeological, and palaeoclimatic evidence, this article reconstructs the broad patterns of plague’s arrival in the southern Red Sea region during the 1430s. It contends that this initial introduction led to the formation of a medium-term reservoir that generated recurrent epidemic waves over the subsequent 150–200 years. This development is attributed to the interplay of environmental and human-driven factors acting together. The study adopts a dual approach: first, it examines how commercial networks across the Red Sea facilitated the spread of the plague; second, it investigates the environmental and topographical shifts in the southern Red Sea between 1370 and 1470 to understand how these conditions allowed the disease to become endemic to the region.

title: Nakai Masakazu and the Revolutionary Potential of Consumption: From Bi-hihyō to the “Logic of the Committee” and Kyoto’s “Housing Problem” in 1930s Japan
abstract: Abstract This article focuses on the prewar theoretical and print activities of Kyoto school philosopher Nakai Masakazu. It spotlights Nakai’s efforts to confront alienation under finance capitalism and inspire a new “critical” and “cooperative” form of mass subjectivity in consumers. The article contributes to extant scholarship in two ways. First, it develops Nakai’s novel interpretation of Marxism and consumer struggle in connection with his mid-1930s article “Logic of the Committee” (“Iinkai no ronri”) and his work on the tabloid-format newspaper Doyōbi (Saturday). Second, it provides a broader picture of Nakai’s philosophical development by showing how these ideas trace back to his involvement with an understudied set of coterie journals from the early 1930s: Bi-hihyō (Aesthetics/Criticism) and Sekai bunka (World Culture). The article divides into three parts, each of which moves across theory and praxis. Part 1 focuses on Nakai’s work on Bi-hihyō and Sekai bunka. It traces the historical development of Nakai’s early philosophy of collectivity, media technology, and specialization and massification in connection with the “crisis” conditions of early 1930s Japan. Part 2 focuses on Nakai’s attempts to develop and consolidate these concepts in the context of finance capitalism in his seminal “Logic of the Committee.” In particular, it shows how Nakai reinterpreted these early philosophical concepts in terms of consumer alienation. Part 3 then focuses on Nakai’s response to …

title: Esperanto on the Radio: Broadcasting Infrastructure and the Politics of Universal Speech in the Japanese Empire
abstract: Abstract This article explores the interface between Esperanto and the radio in the Japanese Empire. Viewing radio as more than simply a mode of conveyance, it examines the tensions that emerged when a universalizing language met a universalizing medium. The following sections explore how new communication infrastructure enabled Esperantists’ claims to political salience. Radio in the Japanese empire helped articulate powerful forecasts of political solidarity, liberated from the restraints of space or state. However, Esperanto on the radio also appeared in ways that deepened the borders of colonial relations and linguistic hierarchies. The article first discusses the history of radio infrastructure in the Japanese Empire and its role in shaping linguistic topography of the 1920s and 1930s. It then turns to a case study of the 1928 “Esperanto Evening” broadcast from colonial Taiwan by Japanese Esperantists. As one of the few surviving examples of when universalizing language and media met, the transcript of this broadcast reveals the limits of Esperanto’s emancipatory reach.

title: The Neighborhood as Refuge: Dignity, Inclusiveness, and Compassion in Takeda Rintarō’s “Kamagasaki” (1933)
abstract: Abstract Kamagasaki, an urban enclave in Osaka, maintains a long history of marginalization that can be traced to the late 1890s. This article examines the representation of Kamagasaki in Osaka writer Takeda Rintarō’s novella “Kamagasaki.” Published in 1933, shortly after the economically prosperous “Greater Osaka” (“Dai Osaka”) period had ended, the story features the underclass and working-class people in the neighborhood of Kamagasaki, revealing how Osaka’s development has concealed issues, including economic exploitation and social division. This article introduces the concepts of “a compassionate participant” instead of adopting existing tropes of observers of city life, such as the flâneur and the “curiosity hunter” (ryōkisha). Through the perspective of such an observer, Takeda represents the issues of poverty, segregation, and homelessness in a humanistic manner. Simultaneously, by constructing various voices for fictional characters in the novella, Takeda highlights the importance of the “internal gaze” and voices from Kamagasaki. This article argues that by emphasizing how the locals value dignity and interpersonal bonds, Takeda’s representations of Kamagasaki subvert the stereotype of urban margins as morally degenerate. Through his conscious resistance to the social stigma imposed on Kamagasaki by dominant national discourse, which reduces Kamagasaki to a place of degeneration and danger, Takeda depicts a neighborhood characterized by shared attachment and …

title: Industrial Lessons Abroad: Chinese Engineers in Britain, 1933–1948
abstract: Abstract: This article explores the dynamic development of the Federation of British Industries Chinese Apprenticeships Scheme from 1933 to 1948, examining how China’s national reconstruction agenda intersected with Britain’s trade-political interests in technology and engineering. It argues that the scheme embodies key features of Sino-British educational, scientific, and cultural initiatives in the 1930s and 1940s—advancing cultural diplomacy while steering China toward purchasing relationships favorable to Britain. Adopting a multi-perspective approach that combines institutional analysis and bio-graphical research, the article moves beyond traditional narratives of modernization, patriotism, and Sino-British friendship to uncover key tensions within this transnational, factory-based initiative, including international competition in foreign manufacturing exports, the mismatch between Chinese engineering graduates and Britain’s apprenticeship system, Britain’s chronic under-resourcing in cultural diplomacy, and Chinese engineers’ frustrations under nationalist statism. It offers insights into Britain’s cultural diplomacy, China’s nation-building efforts, and broader Sino-British trade and cultural exchanges in the twentieth century.

title: Anti-Colonial Activism and Multi-Imperial Entanglements: Reassessing the 1932 Hongkou Bombing Incident in Interwar Shanghai
abstract: Abstract: This article examines the 1932 Hongkou Park Bombing Incident in Shanghai as a critical episode of anti-colonial resistance that reveals the entangled dynamics of empire, nationalism, and global political activism in the interwar period. Despite its historical significance, the incident remains relatively under-studied in English-language scholarship. This article addresses that gap by situating the bombing within the distinctive urban setting of interwar Shanghai. Drawing on multilingual archival sources and press coverage, this study shows how the bombing incident catalyzed a range of responses: it exposed the contra-dictions of British imperial strategy, prompted Franco-Japanese collaboration in colonial policing, and deepened covert support from the Chinese Nationalist Government. This article argues that the Hongkou Incident not only brought into sharp relief existing power differentials but also served as a catalyst for renegotiating power relations and modes of interaction among agents of multiple empires and local Chinese authorities in the city of Shanghai. In doing so, it contributes to global historiographies of anti-colonialism by demonstrating how interwar Shanghai functioned not only as a site of colonial governance and repression but also as a crucible of trans-Asian political mobilization and media discourse.

title: Kita Ikki and Zeng Qi: National Socialism in East Asia, Late 1910s–Early 1930s
abstract: Abstract: This article explores emergent radical political discourse in East Asia driven, at least partially, by regionalized national socialism, which was one of the two most influential revolutionary ideologies, alongside communism, in the early twentieth-century world. Despite a wealth of scholarship about national struggles and communist movements in the political radicalization of East Asia from the late 1910s to the early 1930s, it is still difficult to understand the role national socialism played in this radicalization, as seen in the ascendance of Kita Ikki and Zeng Qi, the two leading national socialists in Japan and China in this era. By comparing Kita’s and Zeng’s transformative ideas, this article documents radical discursive changes.

title: Koreans Skilled Workers in Japan after the East Asian War of 1592–1598: Pak Hoin and Tofu in Early Modern Tosa Domain
abstract: Abstract: This article analyzes the importance of Korean skilled workers in Japan during and after the East Asian War of 1592–1598. By tracing the story of the Korean Pak Hoin and his descendants, this article demonstrates the close relationship between domains and migrants. In doing so, it demonstrates that migrants were not only widespread throughout early Tokugawa Japan, but also that their experiences were highly varied. By placing Hoin’s experience next to that of other Korean migrants, this article identifies some of the factors that influenced migrant experiences and the varying impact they had on their local environments.

title: The Spanish Naval Station in the Pacific: A Frustrated Project of Global Regeneration (1833–1866)
abstract: Abstract: The project to install a permanent naval station on the South American shores of the Pacific attracted the consensus of Spain’s political-intellectual, military, and diplomatic elites during the reign of Isabel II (1844–1868). This article reconstructs the constellation of strategic, economic, legal, and political arguments used by the Spanish monarchy’s diplomatic agents to support the need to station warships in its former Pacific dominions. It also identifies these agents’ socioeconomic coordinates, networks, and interests, evaluating the factual consequences of their attempts to create the station. We will argue that Spanish political elites conceived the naval station as a critical element in the new repertoire of instruments of power necessary for configuring a “second Spanish empire” based on the ideological postulates of navalism, pan-Hispanism, and the imperialism of free trade. This case study allows us to make some theoretical contributions to understanding the crucial functions that naval stations performed as elements of imperial power in the nineteenth century.

title: Listening to Deep Time: Nineteenth-Century Reconstructions of Carboniferous Soundscapes
abstract: This article investigates how nineteenth-century British writers imagined the soundscapes of ancient environments, focusing on the Carboniferous period as a case study. Often framed as the geological era that birthed coal – and by extension, industrial modernity – the Carboniferous served as fertile ground for textual reconstructions of prehistoric environments. While such reconstructions have traditionally privileged the visual, this study foregrounds the auditory, analysing depictions of silence, vegetal rustling and insect sounds in both scientific and popular Victorian writing. Methodologically, the article draws on concepts from sound studies to integrate the auditory into environmental history – proposing ‘Carboniferous silence’ as a rhetorical tool for evoking absence, estrangement and deep temporal distance. Tracing the shift from imagined stillness to the post-1860s integration of fossil-based insect acoustics, it argues that soundscapes functioned as affective and epistemological bridges between the primeval past and the industrial present. title: Building Cisterns to Buffer Water Scarcity. The Road to Public Responsibility for Drinking Water in Amsterdam, 1670–1790
abstract: During extremely cold winters in the Little Ice Age, frozen waterways impeded shipments of fresh water into the city of Amsterdam. With most of the local surface water and groundwater being brackish and polluted, such winters caused drinking-water crises among the poor. Harvesting rainwater to store it in cisterns was an effective form of climate adaptation, provided they were large enough to bridge the frost period. However, building these large underground reservoirs proved to be an enormous challenge. The great unpredictability of the weather complicated the investments and there was no consensus on the question of who was responsible for the vital drinking-water supply. In the second half of the eighteenth century, the city authorities finally undertook to build water tanks, but only under the threat of popular revolt. title: Controlling Thought? China’s Overseas Study-Training Program and Sino-US Conflict, 1943–1944
abstract: On April 24, 1944, Time magazine published an article provocatively titled “CHINA: Embarrassment of a Confucian.” The piece sharply criticized Chen Lifu, China’s minister of education, for extending his “dictatorship over China’s thinkers” to US soil.1 The article was just one in a wave of reports, each denouncing the Chinese government for enforcing fascist-style “thought control” on overseas students. It raised a pointed question: Why was “Free China,” a country fighting fascism, being accused of fascism itself? Beginning in July 1937, Japan’s full-scale invasion drew China into a protracted and devastating war. Under the banner of Sun Yat-sen’s Three Principles of the People (Sānmín Zhǔyì), the Kuomintang (abbreviated KMT, and also called the Guomindang or Nationalist Party) led the government to retreat to Chongqing (Chungking) in the southwest, a mountainous city surrounded by rivers and plagued by shortages and rampant inflation. Chiang Kai-shek, the Chinese leader, struggled to maintain a fragile balance among Japanese encroachment, communist expansion, and internal division.

title: Hidden precarity: post-separation challenges among Japanese migrant women in Australia
abstract: This exploratory study examines post-separation experiences among Japanese migrant women in Australia, addressing a gap in research on partnership-based migration and marital dissolution. Drawing on in-depth interviews with ten participants, the study situates the findings within structural constraints documented among migrant women from non-English-speaking backgrounds, including language-mediated information barriers, administrative burden, uneven access to legal advice and reliance on informal networks when formal pathways are difficult to navigate. It then shows how these broader conditions can take particular forms in this cohort when they intersect with migration pathways and family-role orientations shaped through common (though not universal) features of Japanese socialisation, including strong commitments to familial responsibility, conflict minimisation and privacy. Using ‘migrant capital’ theory (Erel) alongside the analytic lens of ‘institutional invisibility’, the study demonstrates how apparent markers of integration—including tertiary qualifications, professional backgrounds, English proficiency and permanent residency—can obscure domain-specific vulnerabilities that emerge when separation disrupts resources previously mediated through marriage. title: Epistolary endurance: The ‘grammar of separation’ in seventeenth-century letters by Japanese-born Christian women in Batavia
abstract: Abstract This article examines a corpus of seventeenth-century letters written by Japanese-born Christian women exiled to Batavia following Tokugawa Japan’s anti-Christian measures of the late 1630s. Known as jagatara-bumi (Jakarta letters), these texts were produced under conditions of enforced separation, delayed communication, and close surveillance, circulating through Dutch, Chinese, and Nagasaki intermediaries. Situating them within the contexts of Tokugawa persecution, transregional communicative regimes, and early modern epistolary cultures, the article argues that letter-writing functioned as a form of epistolary endurance: a practice of sustaining relational presence across distance and faced with uncertainty. It develops the concept of a ‘grammar of separation’ to describe the historically situated, patterned ways in which rupture was articulated and managed in exile. Rather than reading these letters as transparent records, it treats them as structured practices shaped by convention, constraint, and hybrid religious vocabularies, analysed across emotional, textual, social, and spiritual registers.

title: Machines Writing Histories Using Insect Algorithms: Toward an Age of Environmental Historiography for Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Insect-inspired algorithms have broad appeal in artificial intelligence (AI). They power the labeling, selection, and grouping of data from the past, including the human past. Insect-inspired AI is therefore of interest to historians and, in particular, environmental historians. On an almost separate track, global environmental histories have highlighted the shaping role of capital in driving extractive activities. AI as capital, though, is not the only lens available for seeing artificial insects. Work on green AI, as well as responsible AI more broadly, suggests that another future for the entangled management of data from the past is possible. At present, however, these approaches are largely separate, and they do not accommodate experiences beyond the Global North. In contrast, First Nations’ ontologies provide potential approaches to a nourishing AI in which the social and environmental impacts of algorithms and associated hardware, software and labor systems are considered together, dynamically.

title: Visa status and crime patterns among foreign residents in Japan: quantitative correlation and qualitative insights from Vietnamese migrants
abstract: As the migrant population has grown, the relationship between immigration and crime has become a prominent topic in recent political debates in Japan. Yet despite abundant media and government reports, the issue has received little systematic academic analysis. I examine how visa status shapes patterns of criminal involvement among foreign residents and evaluate the relevance of migration regime theory in the context of Japan’s tightly regulated immigration system. Using data from the National Police Agency (NPA) and the Immigration Services Agency (ISA), I calculate suspect rates and offence composition across major visa categories. Fourteen interviews with Vietnamese migrants who had past encounters with law enforcement provide micro-level insights into offenders’ socio-economic backgrounds and lived experiences. The findings reveal a significant correlation between visa design and crime patterns. Visa statuses that provide stable employment opportunities and long-term migration benefits tend to deter criminal involvement, while restrictive statuses are more strongly associated with immigration-related violations. However, the relationship is not linear: visa leniency does not necessarily protect migrants from financial hardship or social marginalisation. Beyond institutional design, migrants’ limited knowledge of Japanese law and their perceptions of criminality also influence patterns of offending.

title: Soldiers, military settlements, and ideas of progress in the British empire, c. 1750–1840
abstract: Abstract The idea of the military being central to British imperial expansion is nothing new. British armies were both conquerors of colonial territories and institutions through which imperial rule was managed and sustained. In analysing the settlement of demobilised soldiers across Scotland, Trinidad, Sierra Leone, and North India, this article draws attention to the additional significance of the army in colonial concepts of civilisation and human progress. Recruited from among subject populations, the soldiers in these settlements were seen as a means by which British conceits about progress could be evidenced and were tools through which the British state and its proxies hoped to strengthen imperial rule. The article draws attention to the eighteenth-century origins of the interventionist colonial state and examines the broader significance of colonial manpower in British concepts of civilisation and commercial progress.

title: Cross-cultural motherhood: how Chinese newcomer mothers manage school choice anxieties in Japan
abstract: This study examines how Chinese newcomer mothers in Japan experience and manage educational anxieties during school choice. Drawing on Berry’s acculturation model and Lazarus and Folkman’s stress and coping theory, it examines how these mothers navigate tensions between Chinese meritocratic ideals and Japan’s balanced educational norms, amid institutional opacity and familial dynamics. Based on semi-structured interviews with 16 mothers, the findings reveal a cyclical school choice process characterised by reliance on information instability, and relations, generating anxieties across three domains: cultural adaptation, social interfaces, and family mediation. Mothers act as multi-role intermediaries, employing problem-focused and emotion-focused coping strategies shaped by education level, occupation, spousal nationality, and Japanese proficiency. The findings indicate that school-choice anxiety reshapes motherhood in cross-cultural contexts, calling for closer attention to cross-border dynamics of parentocracy in East Asia.

title: Common Reed and Giant Cane: Transnational Plant Lives and Hydro-Modernities in the Socialist Danube Delta
abstract: This article explores the historical emergence of the Danube Delta as part of the larger story of hydro-modernity—that is, the creation of political and scientific representations of dynamic landscapes comprised of waters, silt, plants, animals, and humans. The transformation of the Danube Delta started with the first staging of the landscape as an undeveloped “green sea” in the mid-nineteenth century and then evolved in the twentieth century into a mixed ecological-economic model, reimagined by developing and implementing “stuficultura,” a new techno-science of reeds. Socialist biologists and engineers attempted to modernize the Danube Delta by transforming reeds into an industrial resource, but ultimately, their efforts failed as the reeds proved to be too heterogeneous and difficult to separate from their aquatic ecology. This failure had consequences, providing the backdrop against which other modernization projects would unfold.

title: The Gunboat Philadelphia
abstract: Abstract This essay examines the labor required to defend Lake Champlain from a British invasion in the summer and fall of 1776. Focusing on material culture and documentary evidence related to the Gunboat Philadelphiaand the larger construction projects carried out that season by the Northern Army under Philip Schuyler and Horatio Gates, the essay argues that the Continental Army was a powerful and relatively efficient mobilizer of people and materiel. The piece concludes by discussing several other recent works that approach the American Revolutionary War from the perspective of the labor it commanded, and suggests how this perspective can shape interpretations of the war experience and the US military's role in nation-building in the early national period that followed.
